title: Cybersecurity Foundations
summary: Build a durable mental model of assets, threats, vulnerabilities, risk, controls, least privilege, and layered defense.
roleConnection: These concepts provide the shared language used to explain findings, prioritize risk, select controls, and communicate with technical and business partners.
objectives: Explain confidentiality, integrity, and availability with practical examples
Distinguish assets, threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood, impact, and risk
Compare preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, and compensating controls
Apply least privilege and defense in depth to a simple system design
jdResponsibilities: Assess security risk and explain business impact
Recommend layered safeguards and compensating controls
Protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information
Communicate security principles to technical and nontechnical stakeholders

sections.title: Security protects useful outcomes
paragraphs: Cybersecurity is the practice of managing risk so people and organizations can use technology reliably. It is not a promise that nothing bad will happen. A defender identifies what matters, understands plausible harm, reduces avoidable exposure, watches for trouble, and prepares to recover.

An asset can be information, a service, a device, a person, a process, or reputation. Asset owners describe business importance and acceptable disruption; security practitioners translate that context into protections and evidence. Ownership matters because a control without an accountable decision-maker often becomes stale.
keyPoints: Start with the mission and assets
Security is risk management, not perfect prevention
Owners provide business context
sections.analogy: Security is like protecting a community library: the books, catalog, building, staff, and ability to serve readers all matter.
howTo: List information and dependencies it needs
Ask what failure would matter to users

callout.text: A tool is not the goal; a dependable business outcome is the goal.

sections.title: The CIA triad
paragraphs: The CIA triad means Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability. Confidentiality limits information to authorized people and systems. Integrity preserves accuracy, completeness, and trustworthy change. Availability keeps information and services accessible when authorized users need them.

The three goals can pull in different directions. A highly restrictive control might protect confidentiality but make emergency access too slow. A resilient duplicate system can improve availability but create another copy that must be protected. Good decisions document tradeoffs rather than maximizing one goal blindly.
keyPoints: Confidentiality concerns authorized disclosure
Integrity concerns trustworthy data and change
Availability concerns timely, reliable access
sections.analogy: A sealed, accurate, and open-on-time pharmacy prescription represents confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
howTo: Describe one failure for each CIA goal

sections.title: Threats, vulnerabilities, and risk
paragraphs: A threat is a circumstance or actor that could cause harm. A vulnerability is a weakness that could be used or triggered. Risk combines uncertainty about an event with its consequences; teams often discuss likelihood and impact while acknowledging that numbers are estimates, not facts.

A threat does not automatically create urgent risk, and a vulnerability score is not the whole decision. Exposure, existing safeguards, exploit activity, asset criticality, safety effects, and recovery options alter priority. State assumptions and evidence so another analyst can understand the reasoning.
keyPoints: Threat and vulnerability are different concepts
Risk includes context and consequence
Document evidence and uncertainty
sections.analogy: Rain is a threat, a hole in the roof is a vulnerability, and damage to equipment below is the risk.

sections.title: Controls and least privilege
paragraphs: Controls change risk. Preventive controls reduce the chance of an event, detective controls reveal it, corrective controls limit or repair harm, deterrent controls discourage behavior, and compensating controls provide an alternative when a preferred safeguard is impractical. One control can serve multiple functions.

Least privilege gives identities only the access needed for an approved purpose and duration. It applies to people, services, devices, and automated jobs. Reviews should cover permissions, dormant access, privileged pathways, separation of duties, and a safe process for urgent elevation.
keyPoints: Controls should map to a stated risk
Least privilege includes scope and time
Access reviews need owners and evidence
sections.analogy: A hotel guest receives a key for one room and a limited stay, not a permanent master key.

callout.text: Change access only through authorized processes; classroom designs are not production approvals.

sections.title: Defense in depth and safe practice
paragraphs: Defense in depth layers independent safeguards across identity, endpoint, network, application, data, monitoring, response, and recovery. Layers should address different failure modes. Five copies of the same fragile control are not equivalent to diverse prevention, detection, containment, and restoration capabilities.

In a learning lab, use synthetic assets and reversible settings to practice control selection. In production, changes require an owner, impact analysis, testing, approval, monitoring, and rollback. Never infer that a named employer uses a particular architecture, product, or policy from this course.
keyPoints: Layer diverse controls
Assume individual safeguards can fail
Separate lab exploration from authorized production change
sections.analogy: A castle combines distance, walls, gates, guards, alarms, and supplies rather than relying on one lock.

callout.text: Production controls must be selected from actual requirements and approved architecture, not assumptions.

workflow: Identify the outcome and asset owner
Describe plausible threats and weaknesses
Estimate likelihood and impact with evidence
Select layered controls and accountable owners
Monitor effectiveness and revisit assumptions

quiz.question: Which example is primarily an integrity concern?
options: A customer record is changed to the wrong address
A public website is briefly unavailable
An authorized analyst reads a report
quiz.explanation: Integrity is concerned with the accuracy and trustworthiness of information and changes.

quiz.question: How does a vulnerability differ from a threat?
options: A vulnerability is a weakness; a threat could cause harm using or triggering it
quiz.explanation: The weakness and the circumstance or actor capable of causing harm are distinct inputs to risk.

quiz.question: What best demonstrates least privilege?
options: Granting a task-specific role for an approved period
quiz.explanation: Least privilege limits scope and often duration while preserving an approved business purpose.

quiz.question: Why use defense in depth?
options: It guarantees no incident can occur
It removes the need for recovery
It relies on a single perfect product
Different layers can prevent, reveal, contain, and help recover from failures
quiz.explanation: Diverse layers reduce dependence on any one safeguard and cover different phases of an event.

practice.title: Protect a fictional clinic portal
practice.brief: A synthetic clinic portal stores appointment details and must remain usable during business hours. Design a high-level risk and control view without changing any real system.
tasks: List five assets and an owner for each
Describe one confidentiality, integrity, and availability failure
Separate three threats from three vulnerabilities
Propose layered preventive, detective, and corrective controls
State what would require production approval
answerGuide: Assets include data, identities, application, infrastructure, and service continuity
CIA failures connect to patient privacy, accurate scheduling, and timely access
Threat events are not mislabeled as weaknesses
Controls include identity, validation, logging, backup, and response layers
Any live access or configuration change follows owner review, testing, approval, monitoring, and rollback
practice.safety: Use only the fictional scenario. Do not inspect, test, or change a real healthcare or employer system.

title: Enterprise IT and Service Ownership
summary: Learn how endpoints, servers, directories, identity, virtualization, containers, data flows, owners, and changes fit together.
roleConnection: Security work becomes actionable when an analyst can locate a signal in the wider service, identify its owner, and understand dependencies and approved change paths.
objectives: Differentiate endpoints, servers, virtual machines, containers, and directories
Trace identities and data through a simple enterprise service
Explain why inventory, ownership, dependencies, and lifecycle state affect security
Prepare a safe change request with validation and rollback
jdResponsibilities: Collaborate with infrastructure, application, identity, and data owners
Assess enterprise systems and dependencies during security investigations
Support authorized security configuration and lifecycle improvements
Communicate operational impact and change risk

sections.title: Endpoints, servers, and services
paragraphs: An endpoint is a user-facing or managed device such as a laptop, workstation, or mobile device. A server provides capabilities to other systems, but its physical location may be hidden behind virtual or cloud infrastructure. A service includes technology plus people, processes, suppliers, and data.

Host names, Internet Protocol addresses, and inventory records are clues rather than permanent identity. Devices are rebuilt, addresses change, and services move. Analysts correlate stable asset identifiers, time ranges, owners, and management records before deciding what an event represents.
keyPoints: A service is broader than a machine
Infrastructure identifiers can change
Inventory and time context support attribution
sections.analogy: A restaurant service includes the dining room, kitchen, staff, suppliers, recipes, and reservation system, not just its oven.

sections.title: Directories and Identity and Access Management
paragraphs: A directory stores identities and related attributes. Identity and Access Management, abbreviated IAM, covers identity creation, authentication, authorization, access review, and removal. Human users, service identities, devices, workloads, and external partners may all have identities.

Authentication asks whether a claimant is who or what it says it is; authorization decides what that identity may do. Groups and roles simplify access but can hide inherited privilege. Strong investigations trace direct and nested membership, sign-in evidence, role assignment, and lifecycle events.
keyPoints: Authentication and authorization answer different questions
Nonhuman identities need ownership
Inherited access can be easy to miss
sections.analogy: A passport verifies identity, while a boarding pass authorizes a particular journey.
howTo: Enumerate relevant roles and groups from approved records
Check creation, change, and expiration evidence

callout.text: Do not enumerate identities or alter access outside an approved lab or authorized administrative workflow.

sections.title: Virtualization and containers
paragraphs: A hypervisor lets multiple Virtual Machines, or VMs, use physical hardware while each VM presents a complete guest operating system. Containers usually share a host kernel and package an application with selected dependencies. Images are templates; running containers are disposable instances created from them.

Security boundaries differ by design. Host, hypervisor, image registry, orchestrator, secrets, workload identity, and network policy each require protection. Ephemeral workloads may disappear quickly, so centralized logs, immutable image records, and deployment metadata become important evidence.
keyPoints: VMs and containers isolate differently
Images and runtimes have separate lifecycle concerns
Ephemeral systems require durable external evidence
sections.analogy: VMs resemble separate houses on shared land; containers resemble locked apartments sharing building utilities.
howTo: Identify physical, virtual, and container layers
Locate the image and deployment source

sections.title: Data flows and ownership
paragraphs: A data-flow view shows where information originates, how it is transformed, where it crosses trust boundaries, where it rests, and which consumers receive it. Protocols, identities, encryption, retention, and error paths belong on the map because attackers and accidents follow overlooked paths.

Business owners decide acceptable use and impact. Technical owners operate components. Data owners or stewards define handling expectations. Security teams advise and validate, but they should not silently invent requirements. Ambiguous ownership is itself a risk to raise.
keyPoints: Map sources, transformations, stores, and destinations
Mark trust boundaries and identities
Clarify decision ownership
sections.analogy: A parcel tracking map records sender, sorting hubs, couriers, destination, and handoffs where loss could occur.
howTo: Draw a synthetic request from user to data store

sections.title: Change management and operational safety
paragraphs: Change management makes risk visible before a production modification. A useful change describes purpose, scope, affected services, dependencies, implementation steps, validation, monitoring, owner approval, timing, communications, and a tested rollback path.

Labs encourage experimentation because assets are synthetic and disposable. Production demands evidence and coordination: an apparently harmless logging change can add cost, expose sensitive fields, or overload a service. Emergency processes may be faster, but they still need authorization and retrospective review.
keyPoints: Changes need purpose, validation, monitoring, and rollback
Dependencies turn local changes into service risk
Lab permission does not transfer to production
sections.analogy: A city closes a road only after planning detours, signs, timing, communications, and reopening criteria.
howTo: Test in an approved nonproduction environment

callout.text: This curriculum makes no claim about any employer's internal systems, owners, architecture, or change process.

workflow: Define the service and business owner
Map components, identities, data, and dependencies
Confirm inventory and lifecycle evidence
Assess security and operational impact
Use the authorized change and validation process

quiz.question: What makes a service different from a server?
options: A service includes people, process, data, and dependencies as well as technology
A service always runs on one physical host
quiz.explanation: The service is the broader capability and may span many changing technical components.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes authentication from authorization?
options: Authentication verifies identity; authorization determines allowed actions
quiz.explanation: Verification of identity and permission to act are separate control decisions.

quiz.question: Why are centralized logs especially useful for containers?
options: A short-lived container may disappear before investigation
quiz.explanation: External evidence can survive after an ephemeral workload is replaced or removed.

quiz.question: What belongs in a production change plan?
options: An assumption that dependencies are unaffected
Permission inferred from a lab exercise
Scope, validation, monitoring, authorization, and rollback
quiz.explanation: A controlled change plans both execution and recovery while involving accountable owners.

practice.title: Map a fictional document service
practice.brief: A synthetic document service uses employee laptops, a web tier, a directory, containers, a database, and an external email provider.
tasks: Classify each component and name a technical owner role
Trace sign-in and authorization decisions
Draw the document data flow and trust boundaries
List evidence needed if one container produces an alert
Draft a safe logging-change outline
answerGuide: Endpoints, services, directory, container platform, store, and supplier are distinguished
Authentication, role evaluation, and service identities are shown
Encryption, transformations, storage, and external handoff are visible
Deployment, image, centralized logs, identity, and network evidence are included
The change includes approval, privacy review, test, success measures, monitoring, and rollback
practice.safety: Use the fictional architecture only. Do not query an employer directory, inventory, or platform.

title: Network Fundamentals for Defenders
summary: Follow a packet through names, addresses, routes, ports, transport, web protocols, encryption, and address translation.
roleConnection: Network fluency helps an analyst interpret connections, select useful telemetry, explain exposure, and separate normal service behavior from suspicious patterns.
objectives: Relate Open Systems Interconnection and Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) layers to observable network evidence
Explain addresses, ports, Transmission Control Protocol, User Datagram Protocol, routing, and Network Address Translation
Describe Domain Name System, Hypertext Transfer Protocol, and Transport Layer Security at a beginner level
Trace a packet journey while naming visibility and trust boundaries
jdResponsibilities: Analyze network telemetry and communication paths
Investigate suspicious connections and protocol activity
Assess network exposure and control requirements
Explain technical network findings to service owners

sections.title: Layers as a troubleshooting map
paragraphs: The seven-layer Open Systems Interconnection, or OSI, model is a teaching and troubleshooting framework. The practical TCP/IP model groups similar functions into link, internet, transport, and application layers. Real products do not always fit neatly, but layers help ask where an observation belongs.

A web request depends on local framing, an Internet Protocol packet, a transport conversation, and application messages. A failure at one layer can look like another: a name-resolution error may appear to users as a broken website. Defenders connect evidence across layers instead of treating one log as the whole truth.
keyPoints: Models organize reasoning
One user action creates evidence at multiple layers
Symptoms and root causes can appear at different layers
sections.analogy: Sending a letter involves content, an envelope, a street address, sorting routes, and local delivery.
howTo: Place each available log at a layer

sections.title: Packets, addresses, ports, and transport
paragraphs: A packet carries headers and a portion of data across a network. An Internet Protocol, or IP, address identifies an interface for routing. A port number helps the destination operating system deliver transport traffic to the appropriate application. A familiar port suggests a service but does not prove what the traffic contains.

Transmission Control Protocol, or TCP, establishes a stateful byte stream with sequencing and retransmission. User Datagram Protocol, or UDP, sends independent datagrams with less transport overhead and no built-in delivery guarantee. Applications choose based on their needs and may add reliability themselves.
keyPoints: Addresses support routing; ports support application delivery
TCP offers a reliable ordered stream
UDP offers independent datagrams
sections.analogy: An office building address reaches the property, while a suite number directs delivery to the right tenant.
howTo: Record source and destination IP addresses
Check session state and byte counts
Validate the expected application using authorized evidence

sections.title: DNS and web requests
paragraphs: The Domain Name System, or DNS, translates names into records such as IP addresses and distributes other service information. A resolver may answer from cache or ask other DNS servers. Logs can reveal the querying client, requested name, response, status, and timing, but visibility depends on architecture.

Hypertext Transfer Protocol, or HTTP, uses requests and responses with methods, paths, headers, status codes, and bodies. HTTPS is HTTP protected by Transport Layer Security. Encryption hides much of the content in transit but endpoints and approved metadata sources can still provide security evidence.
keyPoints: DNS maps names and service information
HTTP is a request-response application protocol
HTTPS protects content in transit but does not make a site trustworthy
sections.analogy: DNS is a contact directory; HTTP is the conversation after the number is found.

sections.title: TLS, routing, and NAT
paragraphs: Transport Layer Security, or TLS, negotiates cryptographic protection and authenticates a server through certificates; client authentication is also possible. Analysts may use certificate subjects, issuers, validity, negotiated versions, and endpoint errors without trying to bypass encryption.

Routers forward packets toward networks. Network Address Translation, or NAT, rewrites addresses or ports, often letting many private clients share public addresses. Attribution through NAT requires timestamps, translation records, and sometimes port mappings; a public IP address alone may represent many systems.
keyPoints: TLS protects transport and authenticates endpoints according to configuration
Routing chooses paths between networks
NAT changes observable addresses and complicates attribution
sections.analogy: An office mailroom places one street return address on parcels but keeps an internal ledger of the actual sender.
howTo: Record both pre- and post-translation identifiers if authorized
Avoid attributing a shared address to one person without corroboration

sections.title: A defender's packet journey
paragraphs: A packet journey begins when an application selects a name or address, the operating system chooses transport and a route, the local network frames the packet, intermediaries forward or translate it, and the destination reverses the process. Responses take a route that may not be identical.

Practice packet analysis only with provided captures, your own isolated lab, or explicit authorization. Captures can contain credentials, personal data, and proprietary content. Production capture requires scope, legal and privacy review, secure storage, retention limits, and an approved deletion path.
keyPoints: Trace request and response separately
Correlate clocks and observation points
Packet capture is sensitive and authorization-bound
sections.analogy: Tracking a connecting flight requires departure, transfers, arrival, local time zones, and baggage handoffs.
howTo: Filter to a known lab client and service
Follow DNS, transport setup, TLS, request, and response metadata
Securely remove the lab evidence when done

callout.text: Never capture or inspect traffic on a network you do not own or have explicit permission to monitor.

workflow: Define source, destination, and time window
Resolve names and asset identities
Trace link, IP, transport, and application evidence
Account for routes, proxies, and address translation
Correlate with endpoint and service logs before concluding

commands.title: Read an approved packet capture
commands.code:
Open a provided training capture in Wireshark
Apply: dns or tls
Select one conversation
Follow timestamps and endpoints
commands.explanation: This lab-only sequence uses a supplied capture and avoids collecting live traffic.

quiz.question: What does a destination port primarily help identify?
options: The receiving application or service endpoint
The physical owner of a cable
quiz.explanation: Transport-layer ports help an operating system direct traffic to an application endpoint.

quiz.question: Which characteristic belongs to TCP?
options: It has no concept of ordering
It provides an ordered byte stream with retransmission
quiz.explanation: TCP tracks state, ordering, acknowledgment, and retransmission; encryption is a separate concern.

quiz.question: Why is a public IP address insufficient to identify one internal client behind NAT?
options: Many clients may share it, so translation and port records are needed
quiz.explanation: NAT can multiplex connections from many internal systems through one public address.

quiz.question: What is the safe way to learn packet analysis?
options: Use a provided capture or explicitly authorized isolated lab
quiz.explanation: Network traffic is sensitive; collection and inspection require ownership or explicit authorization.

practice.title: Trace a synthetic browser request
practice.brief: A supplied narrative shows a lab browser resolving training.example, opening a TLS connection, and receiving a page through a NAT gateway.
tasks: Place each event at an OSI or TCP/IP layer
Identify client and server addresses and ports
Explain TCP, DNS, HTTP, and TLS roles
Describe how NAT changes attribution
List corroborating endpoint and server evidence
answerGuide: Events are mapped without treating layers as rigid product boundaries
Source and destination identifiers include a time window
DNS resolution, TCP transport, TLS protection, and HTTP exchange are distinguished
Translation requires timestamped mapping and shared-address caution
Process, resolver, proxy, certificate, and application records provide corroboration
practice.safety: Analyze only the provided synthetic narrative or an explicitly authorized training capture.

title: Network Security and External Connections
summary: Use segmentation, zones, firewalls, proxies, Virtual Private Networks, and connection governance to reduce and monitor network risk.
roleConnection: Network security work combines technical flow review with ownership, policy, vendor coordination, safe implementation, and periodic recertification.
objectives: Design zones and segmentation from trust and business requirements
Interpret ingress, egress, and stateful firewall policy
Compare proxy and Virtual Private Network purposes
Review an external connection from request through retirement
jdResponsibilities: Review network security architecture and firewall policy
Assess and govern external connections and third-party access
Coordinate secure network changes with owners and vendors
Monitor and resolve operational network security issues

sections.title: Zones and segmentation
paragraphs: Segmentation separates systems into zones based on function, sensitivity, exposure, and trust. Boundaries can be physical, virtual, host-based, identity-aware, or application-level. The design should start with allowed business flows rather than drawing a boundary around every device without an operating model.

Segmentation limits reachability and can improve monitoring, but it is not automatic isolation. Shared identity systems, management paths, name services, backups, and cloud control planes may cross zones. Document these dependencies and failure modes.
keyPoints: Zones reflect trust and function
Start from required flows
Management and shared services can cross boundaries
sections.analogy: A hospital separates public waiting areas, treatment rooms, pharmacy storage, and staff-only corridors while preserving necessary movement.
howTo: Ask how a boundary failure is detected

sections.title: Firewalls, direction, and state
paragraphs: A firewall evaluates traffic against policy. Ingress enters a defined boundary; egress leaves it. Direction is relative to that boundary, so diagrams and interface names matter. A rule normally considers source, destination, protocol, port, action, logging, and sometimes application or identity.

A stateful firewall remembers permitted connection state and can allow expected return traffic without a separate broad rule. Policy order, implicit defaults, address groups, translations, and platform behavior affect results. A rule that looks narrow in a ticket can expand through groups.
keyPoints: Define the boundary before using ingress or egress
Stateful policy tracks conversations
Objects, order, and defaults affect effective access
sections.analogy: A staffed gate records an approved delivery entering and recognizes the same truck leaving, rather than treating each direction as unrelated.

sections.title: Proxies and VPNs
paragraphs: A proxy communicates on behalf of a client or server and can enforce policy at the application layer. Forward proxies serve clients; reverse proxies stand before servers. Capabilities may include authentication, filtering, protocol validation, caching, and logging, depending on approved configuration.

A Virtual Private Network, or VPN, creates an encrypted logical connection over another network. It protects traffic in transit but does not make either endpoint trustworthy. Scope routes narrowly, authenticate strongly, monitor use, and define who owns client health and access removal.
keyPoints: Proxies mediate application communication
VPNs protect a path, not every endpoint
Identity, route scope, and lifecycle remain essential
sections.analogy: A proxy is an authorized purchasing agent; a VPN is a guarded tunnel between two entrances.
howTo: Choose mediation or encrypted transport deliberately
Bind access to an owned identity

sections.title: External connection lifecycle
paragraphs: An external connection can link customers, partners, suppliers, remote staff, cloud services, or managed support. A defensible lifecycle covers business sponsor, data classification, architecture, due diligence, technical requirements, approval, implementation, validation, monitoring, periodic review, incident contacts, and retirement.

A supplier name does not establish trust. Confirm contractual and technical responsibilities, support hours, authentication, encryption, source restrictions, logs, resilience, notification expectations, and data return or deletion. Exceptions need rationale, compensating controls, owner acceptance, and expiry.
keyPoints: Every connection needs business and technical ownership
Third-party responsibility must be explicit
Review and retirement are part of the lifecycle
sections.analogy: Issuing a contractor badge requires sponsorship, allowed areas, an expiration date, activity records, and badge return.
howTo: Approve, test, monitor, recertify, and retire

sections.title: Policy review and safe change
paragraphs: A policy review asks whether each flow still supports an approved purpose, is as narrow as practical, has an owner, produces useful evidence, and has an expiry or review date. Usage data can inform cleanup but absence of observed traffic is not proof that a flow is unnecessary.

In a lab, review a fictional rule set and propose improvements. In production, never edit a firewall, proxy, route, or VPN based only on a classroom conclusion. Follow change authorization, test both expected traffic and expected denial, monitor service and security signals, and keep a rollback path.
keyPoints: Policy should be necessary, narrow, owned, logged, and reviewed
Observation supports but does not replace owner validation
Production network changes need authorization and rollback
sections.analogy: A building access list is reviewed with department managers before badges are removed, even if a door was quiet last week.
howTo: Use authorized testing and change controls

callout.text: A production deny or route change can create an outage. Obtain accountable approval and a tested rollback.

workflow: Receive a sponsored connection requirement
Map data, identities, zones, and required flows
Assess architecture, supplier, and policy risk
Approve and implement through controlled change
Validate, monitor, periodically recertify, and retire

quiz.question: What should primarily determine network segmentation?
options: Business flows, sensitivity, function, and trust
A desire for the maximum number of zones
quiz.explanation: Useful segmentation supports required flows while separating systems according to risk and operating context.

quiz.question: What does a stateful firewall add?
options: Awareness of permitted connection state and expected return traffic
quiz.explanation: State tracking relates packets to an established permitted conversation.

quiz.question: Which statement about a VPN is accurate?
options: It proves every endpoint is safe
It removes the need for access review
It protects traffic over a logical path but still needs identity and scope controls
quiz.explanation: Encryption of the path does not establish endpoint health, appropriate authorization, or lifecycle management.

quiz.question: When is an external connection lifecycle complete?
options: As soon as a supplier requests it
After ongoing review and eventual authorized retirement are addressed
quiz.explanation: Connections need governance throughout operation and a controlled end state, not just initial implementation.

practice.title: Review a fictional supplier connection
practice.brief: A synthetic maintenance supplier requests access from fixed public addresses to one application through a managed gateway.
tasks: Identify business and technical owners
Draw zones, trust boundaries, and exact flows
Propose identity, network, logging, and resilience controls
Define validation and rollback
Create review and retirement criteria
answerGuide: A sponsor, application owner, network owner, data owner, and supplier contact are present
The design limits sources, destinations, protocols, direction, and management paths
Strong identity, encrypted transport, least access, health expectations, and useful logs are included
Positive and negative tests plus service monitoring and rollback are defined
Access has expiry, recertification, incident contacts, and secure termination
practice.safety: Keep the exercise on paper. Do not scan a supplier, test public addresses, or change any network control.

title: Security Telemetry and Security Information and Event Management
summary: Turn raw events into normalized, searchable evidence and useful alerts, baselines, and dashboards.
roleConnection: Security analysts use Security Information and Event Management platforms to investigate, monitor, measure, and communicate, while engineers keep telemetry trustworthy and proportionate.
objectives: Explain log events, fields, timestamps, parsing, and normalization
Describe a Security Information and Event Management data path
Write beginner Search Processing Language and Kusto Query Language searches
Evaluate baselines, alert quality, and dashboard purpose
jdResponsibilities: Monitor security events and analyze alerts in SIEM platforms
Develop searches, dashboards, and reporting for defensive operations
Improve telemetry quality, normalization, and retention
Tune alert logic and communicate monitoring coverage

sections.title: Events, fields, and time
paragraphs: A log event is a recorded observation from a source. Useful fields might include event time, ingestion time, host, identity, source and destination, action, outcome, process, request identifier, and raw message. Missing fields are unknown, not automatically benign.

Timestamps need a format, time zone, and known clock behavior. Event time describes when the source says something happened; ingestion time describes when a platform received it. Parsing errors, delay, daylight changes, and skew can scramble a timeline unless the analyst preserves raw evidence.
keyPoints: Events are observations, not perfect truth
Preserve raw data alongside parsed fields
Normalize time before sequencing
sections.analogy: Receipts from several stores use different layouts and clocks; a bookkeeper preserves originals while standardizing key columns.
howTo: Normalize time to Coordinated Universal Time

sections.title: Normalization and baselines
paragraphs: Normalization maps varied source fields and values to a consistent schema. It enables one search across products, but mapping can lose nuance or introduce errors. Keep source-specific identifiers and validate representative events before relying on a normalized field.

A baseline describes expected behavior for a defined population and period. Expected does not mean safe, and unusual does not mean malicious. Account for business cycles, system roles, deployments, maintenance, new users, and incomplete data when comparing observations.
keyPoints: Normalization supports scale but needs validation
Baselines require scope and time
Anomaly is a starting point, not a verdict
sections.analogy: Converting measurements to one unit helps comparison, but a conversion mistake can distort every result.

sections.title: SIEM architecture and data health
paragraphs: A Security Information and Event Management system, abbreviated SIEM, typically collects events, parses and enriches them, stores searchable data, evaluates analytics, and presents investigations, alerts, and dashboards. Queues, collectors, indexes, schemas, and retention differ among products.

A silent source can make a dashboard look calm. Monitor source freshness, volume, parsing success, timestamp quality, duplicate rates, expected fields, pipeline delay, storage limits, and access controls. Sensitive logs require purpose-based access and retention.
keyPoints: The telemetry pipeline has many failure points
Data health is a security signal
Retention and access are governance decisions
sections.analogy: A water system needs source quality, pipes, treatment, storage, pressure monitoring, and safe taps.

sections.title: SPL and KQL search basics
paragraphs: Search Processing Language, or SPL, is associated with Splunk products. Kusto Query Language, or KQL, is used by several Microsoft data services. Vendor-specific syntax here is public and general; it does not imply any employer uses either platform or a particular schema.

A safe beginner search narrows time and source, filters relevant events, selects fields, groups counts, and inspects representative raw records. Start broad enough to understand data, then add conditions one at a time. Validate that field names and values match the actual authorized dataset.
keyPoints: Scope time and data before aggregating
Add filters incrementally
Inspect raw events to validate results
sections.analogy: A library search first chooses the catalog, then topic, date, and format before counting results.

callout.text: Public SPL and KQL examples are generic learning aids, not representations of an employer's tools or schema.

sections.title: Alert quality and dashboards
paragraphs: A useful alert has a clear risk hypothesis, relevant entities, supporting evidence, severity rationale, investigation steps, owner, and measurable outcome. Quality includes true-positive utility, false-positive burden, missed behavior, timeliness, data health, and actionability.

A dashboard should answer named operational questions for a named audience. Counts without denominators, coverage, time context, or definitions can mislead. Production alert and dashboard changes need peer review, controlled deployment, monitoring, and rollback because mistakes can hide real events or overwhelm responders.
keyPoints: Actionability matters as much as volume
Dashboards need audience and questions
Monitoring-content changes are production changes
sections.analogy: A smoke alarm must detect meaningful smoke promptly without sounding every time toast is made.
howTo: Write the detection or reporting question
Test with representative benign and positive cases
Deploy through approved monitoring and rollback

callout.text: Never suppress or alter a production alert solely to make metrics look cleaner.

workflow: Define a defensive question and required evidence
Confirm authorized sources, fields, time, and data health
Search and inspect representative raw events
Evaluate context, baseline, and alternative explanations
Document findings and improve content through controlled change

index=training sourcetype=synthetic_auth earliest=-24h
| stats count by user, outcome
| sort - count

quiz.question: What should an analyst do before sequencing events from different sources?
options: Normalize timestamps and account for zones, delay, and skew
Assume every source uses local time
quiz.explanation: Timeline quality depends on understood clocks and preserved source evidence.

quiz.question: Why preserve raw events after normalization?
options: To validate mappings and retain source nuance
To guarantee the source is correct
quiz.explanation: Raw evidence helps analysts detect parsing errors and inspect details not represented in the common schema.

quiz.question: What does a quiet dashboard prove?
options: Only that few displayed results were produced; pipeline health still needs verification
quiz.explanation: Missing or delayed telemetry can create false calm, so source and pipeline health are required context.

quiz.question: Which is a safe production alert-tuning practice?
options: Disable a noisy rule immediately without recording it
Judge quality only by alert count
Use an unreviewed query copied from a forum
Test, peer review, monitor outcomes, and maintain rollback
quiz.explanation: Controlled changes reduce the risk of either missed detection or responder overload.

practice.title: Investigate a synthetic sign-in spike
practice.brief: A fictional SIEM dataset shows an increase in failed sign-ins and a recent parser update.
tasks: Verify source freshness, parsing, and event versus ingestion time
Write a bounded grouping query
Compare the spike with a scoped baseline
Inspect representative raw failures and successes
Recommend either investigation or controlled content repair
answerGuide: Pipeline health and parser change are checked before interpreting volume
The query uses explicit time, source, identity, outcome, and counts
The baseline considers population and normal cycles
Raw samples validate fields and reveal alternative explanations
The recommendation states evidence, uncertainty, owner, validation, monitoring, and rollback
practice.safety: Use only the synthetic dataset. Do not paste real identities, events, or proprietary queries into the exercise.

title: Endpoint Telemetry and Endpoint Detection and Response
summary: Interpret endpoint processes, parent-child relationships, persistence-relevant changes, network activity, and Endpoint Detection and Response workflows.
roleConnection: Endpoint evidence helps analysts validate alerts, scope affected hosts and identities, preserve evidence, and coordinate containment with system owners.
objectives: Recognize common endpoint telemetry and its limitations
Build and question a process tree using parent-child evidence
Explain System Monitor (Sysmon) and Endpoint Detection and Response concepts
Use a safe triage workflow without making unsupported claims
jdResponsibilities: Investigate endpoint alerts and suspicious process activity
Use endpoint detection and response telemetry for triage and scoping
Coordinate authorized containment and evidence preservation
Improve endpoint visibility and alert quality

sections.title: Endpoint evidence
paragraphs: Endpoint telemetry can record process creation, image metadata, command lines, file activity, registry or configuration change, authentication, network connections, module loading, and security-product observations. Exact events depend on operating system, policy, version, and product.

Telemetry is selective, not a recording of everything. Sensors can be delayed, disabled, misconfigured, or unable to observe activity at another layer. Preserve source, collection time, host identity, policy state, and raw records when drawing conclusions.
keyPoints: Endpoint evidence varies by source and policy
Absence of an event is not proof of absence
Host identity and sensor health are part of context
sections.analogy: A building's badge log records selected door events, not every movement inside every room.
howTo: Collect relevant process, file, identity, and network records

sections.title: Processes and parent-child relationships
paragraphs: A process is a running instance of a program. Process creation evidence can include executable path, hash, signer, command line, user, parent identifier, and start time. Parent-child relationships support a process tree that explains how activity began and what followed.

Unusual parentage is a lead, not a conviction. Software updaters, management agents, scripts, and user actions create surprising trees. Validate file provenance, signature, prevalence, role, nearby events, and expected administration before assigning intent.
keyPoints: Program files and running processes are different
Process trees add causal context
Unusual does not automatically mean malicious
sections.analogy: A family tree shows relationships but does not explain motives without a broader story.
howTo: Anchor a process by host, identifier, and time
Review path, hash, signer, identity, and arguments

sections.title: Sysmon concepts
paragraphs: System Monitor, commonly called Sysmon, is a Microsoft Sysinternals service and driver that records selected Windows activity to an event log. Public event types include process creation, network connection, image load, file, registry, and process-access observations, depending on configuration.

Sysmon does not analyze intent by itself. Configuration choices affect visibility, performance, volume, and privacy. In a lab, read supplied Sysmon records. Deploying or changing production collection requires endpoint ownership, testing, capacity planning, privacy review, approval, and rollback.
keyPoints: Sysmon produces configurable telemetry
Event meaning depends on configuration and context
Collection changes can affect performance and privacy
sections.analogy: A configurable security camera records selected doors and detail levels; placement determines what can later be reviewed.
howTo: Validate enabled fields in lab data
Escalate proposed production collection through change control

callout.text: Do not deploy or reconfigure endpoint telemetry on a production system as a classroom exercise.

sections.title: EDR workflow concepts
paragraphs: Endpoint Detection and Response, abbreviated EDR, combines endpoint telemetry with search, analytics, alerting, investigation, and response capabilities. Common conceptual actions include reviewing detections, searching related hosts, building timelines, collecting approved evidence, isolating a host, and releasing containment.

Specific interfaces and capabilities vary. CrowdStrike University is included as vendor training, but any product details are public and general and do not claim that an employer uses CrowdStrike or a particular workflow. Product access and response actions depend on organizational authorization.
keyPoints: EDR joins visibility, analytics, and response
Vendor interfaces and entitlements vary
Response actions require explicit authority
sections.analogy: EDR is a vehicle dashboard plus a service console: it shows signals, supports diagnosis, and may offer controlled interventions.
howTo: Validate host, identity, process, and time
Recommend rather than execute containment unless authorized

callout.text: Vendor-specific material is public/general and makes no claim about ExxonMobil or any employer's internal tooling.

sections.title: Triage, containment, and boundaries
paragraphs: Triage determines whether the signal is understood, relevant, and urgent. Record the alert hypothesis, process lineage, affected identity, network activity, file evidence, host role, sensor health, and alternative explanations. Scope laterally using approved telemetry rather than assuming one host is the whole event.

Host isolation can disrupt operations, evidence collection, remote access, safety functions, or recovery. In a lab, describe the decision. In production, follow incident authority, consult asset owners when time allows, preserve evidence, document the reason and time, verify effect, and define release criteria.
keyPoints: Triage tests a hypothesis
Scope across related entities
Containment balances harm, evidence, and operations
sections.analogy: Closing a bridge may stop danger but can block emergency vehicles, so the decision needs authority and impact awareness.
howTo: Assess host criticality and active harm
Verify, monitor, document, and plan release

workflow: Validate the alert, endpoint identity, and sensor health
Build process and event context around the signal
Pivot to related identities, files, connections, and hosts
Assess confidence, severity, scope, and operational impact
Coordinate authorized containment, evidence, recovery, and documentation

commands.title: Review a synthetic process event

$event | Select-Object Time, Host, User, ParentImage, Image, CommandLine
commands.explanation: This read-only lab command displays selected fields from a supplied synthetic JSON file; it does not query a live endpoint.

quiz.question: What does endpoint telemetry represent?
options: Selected observations shaped by source and policy
A complete replay of everything on a host
Proof that every unlogged action was benign
quiz.explanation: Sensors record configured observations and have gaps, health states, and context requirements.

quiz.question: What is the best interpretation of an unusual parent-child process relationship?
options: A lead to validate with provenance, context, and related evidence
A reason to delete the child process
quiz.explanation: Process relationships are valuable context, but legitimate tools can create uncommon patterns.

quiz.question: What is Sysmon?
quiz.explanation: Sysmon records selected Windows events according to configuration; analysis and response remain separate.

quiz.question: What should happen before production host isolation?
options: Assume isolation has no business impact
Follow incident authority and assess urgency, evidence, and operational impact
quiz.explanation: Containment is a consequential production action requiring authorization and informed tradeoffs.

practice.title: Triage a synthetic endpoint alert
practice.brief: A fictional design workstation launches a rare signed utility from an approved software-management parent and connects to an internal package server.
tasks: Validate host, user, sensor, and timestamps
Build the process tree and list relevant fields
Correlate file, network, and deployment evidence
Write malicious and benign hypotheses
Recommend a proportionate next action
answerGuide: Identity, role, health, clock, and source are established
Parent, process, children, path, hash, signer, arguments, and identifiers are recorded
Package source, change record, prevalence, and destination ownership are checked
The signed file is not assumed safe and unusual behavior is not assumed malicious
The recommendation states confidence and avoids disruptive containment without authorization
practice.safety: Use only synthetic endpoint events. Do not run unknown files, query a real EDR tenant, or isolate a live host.

title: Incident Response and Recovery
summary: Prepare for, detect, respond to, and recover from incidents while managing severity, scope, evidence, containment, root cause, and learning.
roleConnection: Incident responders turn uncertain signals into coordinated decisions that limit harm, preserve trustworthy evidence, restore services, and improve future resilience.
objectives: Describe preparation, detection, response, and recovery as connected activities
Assess severity and scope using evidence and business impact
Balance containment, evidence preservation, and operational needs
Conduct root cause analysis and lessons learned aligned to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
jdResponsibilities: Lead or support cybersecurity incident investigation and response
Assess incident severity, impact, scope, and escalation needs
Coordinate containment, recovery, communications, and evidence handling
Perform root cause analysis and drive lessons-learned improvements

sections.title: Preparation makes response possible
paragraphs: Preparation establishes roles, decision authority, contacts, playbooks, evidence access, communications, exercises, logging, backups, and recovery expectations before pressure arrives. It also identifies legal, privacy, safety, regulatory, supplier, and business-continuity partners.

NIST Cybersecurity Framework, or CSF, 2.0 describes Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover outcomes. Response is not an isolated team: governance sets authority, identification supplies context, protection reduces exposure, detection produces signals, and recovery restores and improves.
keyPoints: Authority and contacts should be known before an incident
Response depends on all NIST CSF 2.0 functions
Exercises reveal gaps safely
sections.analogy: A fire drill tests exits, roles, communications, and accountability before smoke makes every decision harder.

sections.title: Detection, declaration, and severity
paragraphs: An event is an observable occurrence. An alert is a signal selected for review. An incident is an occurrence that actually or imminently jeopardizes objectives according to organizational criteria. Triage gathers enough evidence to close, continue, escalate, or declare without pretending uncertainty has disappeared.

Severity combines current and potential impact, affected assets and data, operational or safety consequences, adversary activity, spread, urgency, and recovery difficulty. Priority can change as evidence develops. Use defined criteria and record why a level was chosen.
keyPoints: Event, alert, and incident are not synonyms
Declaration follows criteria and authority
Severity is revisited as impact and scope change
sections.analogy: A weather sensor reading becomes a warning only after context shows a dangerous storm is plausible.
howTo: Record uncertainty and next review point

sections.title: Scope, evidence, and timeline
paragraphs: Scoping asks which identities, hosts, applications, accounts, data, locations, and time periods are affected. Start from known indicators and behaviors, then pivot through reliable relationships. Expand deliberately; broad unstructured collection can overwhelm responders and expose unnecessary data.

A timeline separates source event time, observed time, collection time, analyst action, and business impact. Preserve raw evidence, provenance, time-zone handling, query versions, and acquisition details. If evidence may support disciplinary, legal, or regulatory action, engage the appropriate specialists.
keyPoints: Scope uses entities, relationships, and time
Timelines distinguish multiple kinds of time
Evidence provenance supports trust
sections.analogy: Mapping an illness outbreak starts with confirmed cases, contacts, places, and dates rather than testing an entire city without a plan.
howTo: Review scope with owners and responders

sections.title: Containment, eradication, and recovery
paragraphs: Containment limits ongoing harm. Eradication removes the condition enabling the incident. Recovery restores trusted operation and watches for recurrence. These activities may overlap: a team might revoke one credential immediately, preserve a host, rebuild another, and add temporary monitoring.

Actions can destroy evidence or interrupt critical operations. Choose short- and long-term containment with incident authority and asset owners when circumstances permit. Define validation, dependencies, communication, rollback, and release criteria. Never treat a lab response button as permission to act in production.
keyPoints: Containment, eradication, and recovery solve different needs
Response actions have operational side effects
Restoration requires trust criteria and monitoring
sections.analogy: Stopping a water leak, replacing the broken pipe, drying the building, and checking for mold are related but distinct tasks.
howTo: Assess active harm and operational criticality
Authorize and execute the least harmful effective action

callout.text: Production containment and recovery actions require assigned incident authority and operational coordination.

sections.title: Root cause and lessons learned
paragraphs: Root Cause Analysis, or RCA, looks beyond the first technical failure to contributing conditions such as design, process, training, incentives, ownership, monitoring, and recovery readiness. Avoid a single-person blame narrative when system improvements could prevent recurrence or reduce impact.

A lessons-learned review should be psychologically safe, evidence-based, time-bounded, and connected to accountable actions. Capture what happened, what worked, what hindered response, detection and recovery gaps, risk decisions, owners, deadlines, and a way to verify completion.
keyPoints: Root cause may include several contributing conditions
Learning should improve systems, not assign simplistic blame
Actions need owners and verification
sections.analogy: An aviation review studies equipment, procedures, conditions, training, and communication rather than stopping at the last person who touched a control.
howTo: Assign owners, dates, measures, and follow-up

callout.text: A closed incident is not fully learned from until agreed improvements are verified.

workflow: Prepare roles, evidence, communications, and recovery capabilities
Detect, validate, declare, and set initial severity
Investigate timeline, impact, and scope
Contain, eradicate, recover, and monitor under authority
Complete root cause analysis and verify lessons-learned actions

quiz.question: What is the best reason to exercise incident response before an incident?
options: To reveal authority, access, evidence, and coordination gaps safely
To guarantee incidents will not occur
quiz.explanation: Exercises test readiness and create improvement actions before real harm and time pressure.

quiz.question: How should incident severity be handled?
options: Set permanently from the first alert name
Base it on evidence and impact, then revisit as scope changes
Choose the highest level for every alert
Measure it only by event count
quiz.explanation: Severity reflects current evidence, potential consequences, urgency, and scope, all of which can change.

quiz.question: Why might immediate containment be delayed briefly?
options: Only public incidents can be contained
A specific action may destroy evidence or cause greater operational harm
Evidence has no value during response
quiz.explanation: Responders balance ongoing harm with safety, operations, evidence, and the effectiveness of available actions.

quiz.question: What makes a lessons-learned action effective?
options: It has no deadline so it remains flexible
It stays separate from risk governance
It has an owner, due date, expected outcome, and verification
quiz.explanation: Accountability and evidence of completion turn learning into sustained improvement.

practice.title: Respond to a fictional account compromise
practice.brief: A synthetic cloud account shows an unusual sign-in followed by approved-document downloads. The employee is traveling, and evidence is incomplete.
tasks: Validate the alert and decide whether declaration criteria may be met
Assign initial severity and list assumptions
Build a scoping and evidence plan
Recommend containment and recovery with operational checks
Draft three lessons-learned actions
answerGuide: The response distinguishes event, alert, and incident and contacts the identity and data owners
Severity considers data, account privilege, activity, confidence, and travel context
Scope covers identity sessions, devices, applications, documents, related accounts, and time
Session and credential actions preserve evidence, use authority, validate user impact, and monitor recovery
Actions address identity controls, telemetry, travel validation, process, and measurable follow-up
practice.safety: Use only the fictional records. Do not reset a real account, contact a real employee, or access live cloud logs.

title: Cyber Threat Intelligence
summary: Transform evaluated information into tactical, operational, or strategic intelligence using behavioral frameworks and a repeatable lifecycle.
roleConnection: Threat intelligence helps defenders prioritize relevant behaviors, enrich investigations, shape detections, brief leaders, and avoid overreacting to unreliable indicators.
objectives: Differentiate Indicators of Compromise from Indicators of Attack
Tailor tactical, operational, and strategic intelligence to decisions
Use MITRE ATT&CK and the Diamond Model as analytical aids
Evaluate sources and apply the intelligence lifecycle
jdResponsibilities: Analyze cyber threat intelligence and assess organizational relevance
Enrich incidents, hunts, and detections with adversary behavior context
Produce timely intelligence for technical and leadership audiences
Evaluate external sources, vendors, and information-sharing constraints

sections.title: Information becomes intelligence
paragraphs: Threat information includes observations, claims, reports, and data about harmful actors or activity. Intelligence is information analyzed for a decision, with relevance, confidence, assumptions, and timeliness made clear. Copying a feed into a platform is collection, not completed analysis.

Start with a requirement: for example, which behaviors should a sector watch this quarter, or whether a reported campaign changes an active incident. Without a consumer and decision, analysts can produce large volumes that expire without reducing risk.
keyPoints: Intelligence serves a decision
Analysis adds relevance and confidence
Requirements prevent collection without purpose
sections.analogy: A pile of weather readings becomes a forecast only after analysis for a place, time, and decision.

sections.title: IOC, IOA, and intelligence levels
paragraphs: An Indicator of Compromise, or IOC, is observable evidence associated with possible compromise, such as a hash, domain, address, or artifact. An Indicator of Attack, or IOA, emphasizes behavior suggesting malicious activity, such as an unexpected sequence of discovery and remote access actions.

Tactical intelligence supports near-term detection with observables and behaviors. Operational intelligence informs campaigns and response. Strategic intelligence explains trends, implications, and choices for leaders. The same source may support all three, but language, detail, confidence, and horizon differ.
keyPoints: IOCs are clues requiring context
IOAs emphasize behavior
Intelligence level follows the consumer's decision horizon
sections.analogy: A footprint is an indicator; a pattern of stalking behavior conveys intent; a regional safety trend informs long-term planning.
howTo: Choose tactical, operational, or strategic audience

sections.title: ATT&CK and the Diamond Model
paragraphs: MITRE ATT&CK is a public knowledge base organizing observed adversary tactics and techniques. It supports a common behavioral vocabulary for intelligence, detection, hunting, and coverage discussions. A technique mapping is a hypothesis that should cite evidence; ATT&CK is not a list of mandatory detections.

The Diamond Model relates adversary, capability, infrastructure, and victim in an intrusion event. Analysts can pivot among these features and consider social, technical, and temporal context. The model structures questions without proving attribution.
keyPoints: ATT&CK describes behavior using a shared vocabulary
Mappings require evidence
The Diamond Model supports relationship pivots, not automatic attribution
sections.analogy: A map legend gives travelers common symbols, while a route sketch connects who traveled, with what, through where, and toward whom.
howTo: Extract a behavior from a report

sections.title: Source evaluation and confidence
paragraphs: Evaluate a source's access, expertise, history, incentives, transparency, independence, and proximity to the observation. Separately assess claim credibility through corroboration, technical consistency, recency, and alternative explanations. A reputable publisher can still relay an uncertain claim.

Use calibrated language such as low, moderate, or high confidence according to a defined scheme. Distinguish fact, source claim, inference, and assumption. Respect handling restrictions, privacy, licensing, and information-sharing agreements.
keyPoints: Source reliability and claim credibility are related but separate
Confidence needs a shared meaning
Handling constraints travel with information
sections.analogy: A trusted newspaper may quote an anonymous witness; readers evaluate the publisher and the specific claim separately.

sections.title: The intelligence lifecycle
paragraphs: The intelligence lifecycle is commonly described as direction, collection, processing, analysis, dissemination, and feedback. In practice it loops: feedback sharpens requirements, new collection changes analysis, and expiring indicators trigger updates or withdrawal.

Use authorized public, licensed, or organizational sources. Do not access restricted systems, interact with threat actors, buy illicit data, or collect personal information as a learning exercise. Production blocking based on intelligence requires validation, owner approval, impact review, monitoring, and rollback.
keyPoints: Direction and feedback keep intelligence relevant
Indicators need lifecycle and expiry
Collection and defensive action have legal and operational boundaries
sections.analogy: A restaurant repeatedly asks diners what they need, sources ingredients, prepares a meal, serves it, and uses feedback to improve.
howTo: Disseminate, receive feedback, and retire stale content

callout.text: Threat-intelligence learning never authorizes covert contact, illicit access, or unreviewed production blocking.

workflow: Direct work with a consumer, decision, and deadline
Collect from authorized sources and preserve provenance
Process and evaluate source, claim, relevance, and timeliness
Analyze behavior, relationships, alternatives, and confidence
Disseminate with handling, actions, expiry, and feedback

quiz.question: What turns threat information into intelligence?
options: Analysis that supports a defined decision with relevance and confidence
Having a long list of addresses
quiz.explanation: Intelligence is decision-focused analysis, not raw collection volume.

quiz.question: How does an IOA generally differ from an IOC?
options: An IOA is always a file hash
An IOA emphasizes behavior suggesting attack activity
quiz.explanation: Behavioral indicators can remain useful even as specific infrastructure or files change.

quiz.question: What does an ATT&CK mapping establish?
options: That every organization must deploy one product
A behavioral classification supported to the extent of the evidence
quiz.explanation: ATT&CK provides vocabulary; the analyst remains responsible for evidentiary support and uncertainty.

quiz.question: Which is the safest response to a newly reported malicious domain?
options: Assume every historical visitor is compromised
Validate provenance, relevance, collisions, and impact before authorized action
quiz.explanation: Indicators can be stale, shared, mistyped, or irrelevant; action should be controlled and evidence-based.

practice.title: Assess a fictional campaign report
practice.brief: A synthetic public report claims a group targets manufacturers using newly registered domains and scripted archive collection.
tasks: Write one tactical and one strategic intelligence requirement
Separate report claims, facts, inferences, and assumptions
Evaluate source and claim confidence
Map supported behavior to ATT&CK and Diamond Model features
Recommend collection, dissemination, and expiry
answerGuide: Requirements name consumers, decisions, and time horizons
The answer does not present attribution claims as established fact
Reliability, corroboration, recency, alternatives, and gaps shape confidence
Mappings use only described behavior and mark unknowns
Recommendations use authorized logs and review any production detection or blocking change
practice.safety: Use the synthetic report and public frameworks only. Do not contact actors, visit suspicious infrastructure, or collect unauthorized data.

title: Hypothesis-Driven Threat Hunting
summary: Form testable defensive hypotheses, understand telemetry and baselines, pivot through evidence, build timelines, and document both positive and negative findings.
roleConnection: Threat hunters proactively examine uncertainty and coverage gaps, then turn supported findings into incidents, engineering improvements, or documented knowledge.
objectives: Write a bounded and testable hunting hypothesis
Evaluate required telemetry, coverage, and baseline limits
Pivot among entities while controlling scope
Document positive, negative, and inconclusive findings accurately
jdResponsibilities: Conduct proactive threat hunts using hypotheses and behavioral analytics
Build timelines and pivot across endpoint, identity, network, and cloud data
Identify detection and telemetry gaps
Document hunt results and transition confirmed findings to response

sections.title: From question to hypothesis
paragraphs: A hunt is a planned investigation for activity not already resolved by alerts. A useful hypothesis links a plausible behavior to an environment and observable evidence: for example, if a compromised service identity is being used interactively, then sign-in type and resource patterns should differ from its established workload behavior.

A hypothesis is not a conclusion. Define population, period, expected evidence, required coverage, falsifying observations, safety limits, and stop conditions. Broad questions such as finding all threats are not testable and tend to produce uncontrolled data exploration.
keyPoints: Hunts begin with bounded uncertainty
Hypotheses predict observable evidence
Falsification and stop conditions reduce confirmation bias
sections.analogy: A scientist predicts what a measurement should show and what would disprove the idea before running the experiment.

sections.title: Telemetry and baseline readiness
paragraphs: Before querying, map each predicted behavior to data sources, fields, retention, health, clock quality, and known blind spots. A negative result means only that the chosen method found no matching evidence within available coverage.

Build a baseline for a comparable population and meaningful time range. Peer groups, host roles, identity types, maintenance windows, travel, and software rollouts can matter. Document changes in telemetry or population that could create an apparent anomaly.
keyPoints: Coverage bounds every hunt conclusion
Negative results are qualified by method and visibility
Baselines need comparable populations
sections.analogy: Not seeing fish through a small window does not prove the lake is empty.

sections.title: Queries and pivots
paragraphs: Begin with the least expensive query that can test the hypothesis, using explicit time and population. Inspect representative raw events before aggregating. Track query versions, field assumptions, and result counts so the work can be reviewed and repeated.

A pivot follows a justified relationship such as identity to host, process to hash, domain to connection, or cloud session to resource. Every pivot can widen scope and expose more sensitive data. State why it is relevant and stop when marginal value no longer supports cost or privacy impact.
keyPoints: Bound queries and validate raw data
Pivots need an evidentiary reason
Reproducibility includes query versions and assumptions
sections.analogy: Following footnotes is useful when each citation relates to the question; opening every book in the library is not.
howTo: Review scope and privacy as the hunt expands

sections.title: Timeline and finding evaluation
paragraphs: A hunt timeline combines normalized event times with source, entity, action, outcome, and confidence. Look for sequence and causality without forcing every nearby event into one story. Separate confirmed facts, analytical inferences, and unanswered questions.

Evaluate alternative explanations through targeted checks. A positive finding may warrant incident response; a benign explanation may still expose a detection or documentation gap. An inconclusive result may justify telemetry improvement rather than endless searching.
keyPoints: Chronology does not automatically prove causality
Alternatives deserve explicit tests
Inconclusive can be a valid outcome
sections.analogy: Editing a documentary requires timestamps and sources, but adjacent scenes do not prove one caused the other.
howTo: Choose escalation, closure, or coverage improvement

sections.title: Documenting and operationalizing
paragraphs: A hunt report records hypothesis, rationale, scope, data coverage, queries, pivots, findings, limitations, confidence, and recommended actions. Positive, negative, and inconclusive outcomes all create organizational knowledge when their boundaries are clear.

Do not quietly convert a hunt query into a production alert. Detection content needs requirements, testing, peer review, ownership, monitoring, and rollback. Do not execute response actions unless the hunt has been transitioned through authorized incident procedures.
keyPoints: Report methods and limits, not just conclusions
Negative hunts still inform coverage and future work
Operationalization follows controlled engineering and response processes
sections.analogy: A medical study publishes methods and limitations so others can interpret even a result that found no effect.
howTo: Attach saved query versions or references
Transition actions to incident or engineering owners

callout.text: Hunt access is not permission to contain systems or deploy production detections.

workflow: Form a testable hypothesis with scope and falsifiers
Validate telemetry, coverage, and baseline
Run bounded queries and evidence-based pivots
Build a timeline and test alternative explanations
Report positive, negative, or inconclusive results and route actions

commands.title: Summarize fictional service-identity sign-ins

| where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-01-01) .. datetime(2026-01-08))
| where IdentityType == "Service"
