quiz.question: Which is the strongest hunting hypothesis?
options: If a service identity is used interactively, its sign-in type and resource pattern will differ from its workload baseline
Assume all service identities are compromised
quiz.explanation: A strong hypothesis predicts observable evidence in a bounded population and can be tested.

quiz.question: What does a hunt with no matching results establish?
options: The method found no match within the documented scope and coverage
quiz.explanation: Negative results are constrained by data quality, retention, query logic, scope, and time.

quiz.question: When is a pivot justified?
options: Only when a vendor suggests it
When a relationship is relevant to testing the hypothesis
When it exposes the largest population
quiz.explanation: Evidence-based pivots control scope and preserve analytical focus.

quiz.question: What should happen to a promising hunt query before it becomes an alert?
options: Use the detection engineering review, test, deployment, monitoring, and rollback process
quiz.explanation: A hunt query and a reliable production detection have different quality and operational requirements.

practice.title: Hunt for fictional interactive service use
practice.brief: A synthetic dataset contains workload and interactive sign-ins for service and human identities over seven days.
tasks: Write the hypothesis, falsifiers, scope, and stop conditions
Assess dataset fields, health, and blind spots
Build a baseline by identity type and resource
Pivot on two justified anomalies and build a timeline
Write positive, negative, and inconclusive result language
answerGuide: The hypothesis predicts observable behavior without presuming compromise
Coverage, retention, time, field meaning, and missing device context are recorded
Peer comparisons do not mix human and service identities blindly
Pivots are justified and facts remain separate from inferences
Each outcome is qualified and routed appropriately to response, engineering, or closure
practice.safety: Use only the provided synthetic table. Do not hunt real identities or broaden access beyond an approved case.

title: Digital Forensics and Evidence Integrity
summary: Preserve and analyze disk, memory, network, and service artifacts using order of volatility, chain of custody, timelines, and evidence-integrity practices.
roleConnection: Forensic discipline lets responders answer what happened while preserving evidence trustworthiness and avoiding accidental alteration or overstatement.
objectives: Prioritize evidence using order of volatility and incident needs
Distinguish forensic acquisition from analysis
Maintain chain of custody and verify evidence integrity
Build a source-aware timeline from disk, memory, network, and service artifacts
jdResponsibilities: Collect and analyze authorized digital evidence
Preserve chain of custody and evidence integrity
Support incident scoping and root cause analysis with forensic artifacts
Communicate forensic findings, limitations, and confidence

sections.title: Forensic questions and authority
paragraphs: Digital forensics uses repeatable methods to identify, preserve, collect, examine, analyze, and report digital evidence. Begin with authorized questions and scope. Different purposes such as rapid incident response, internal review, litigation, or regulatory inquiry can require different specialists and procedures.

Evidence can contain personal, privileged, regulated, or unrelated information. Collect proportionately, restrict access, document purpose, follow retention and legal direction, and avoid exploring data merely because it is available.
keyPoints: Purpose and authority shape forensic work
Repeatability supports trustworthy conclusions
Minimize unrelated sensitive collection
sections.analogy: A laboratory examines samples tied to a case question, labels them carefully, and does not test unrelated material out of curiosity.
howTo: Define systems, data, and time scope

sections.title: Order of volatility
paragraphs: Order of volatility prioritizes information likely to disappear first. Running memory, active connections, processes, and temporary state may change quickly; disks, centralized logs, backups, and archival records are usually more durable. Exact order depends on the system and incident.

Collecting volatile data changes the system, while shutting down can destroy it. Responders balance evidentiary value, active harm, operational safety, available expertise, and approved procedures. Do not improvise acquisition on a critical live system.
keyPoints: Volatile evidence can vanish rapidly
Acquisition itself changes state
Safety and incident objectives influence collection order
sections.analogy: At an outdoor scene, photograph footprints before rain while durable objects can be cataloged later.
howTo: Assess active harm and system criticality
Record system time and collector effects

callout.text: Live acquisition can disrupt systems and alter evidence; use authorized specialists and procedures.

sections.title: Acquisition, hashing, and chain of custody
paragraphs: Acquisition creates a controlled copy or export for later examination; analysis interprets that evidence. Work from verified copies where possible and preserve the original. A cryptographic hash is a digest used to detect whether bytes changed, not proof that the original source was truthful.

Chain of custody records what was collected, by whom, when, where, how, under what authority, with which tool and version, integrity values, storage, access, transfer, and disposition. Labels and timestamps should be unambiguous and consistent.
keyPoints: Acquisition and analysis are distinct
Hashes detect byte changes
Chain of custody records control and handling
sections.analogy: A sealed evidence bag has a unique label and transfer log; the seal detects opening but does not explain how the item was created.
howTo: Log storage, access, transfer, and disposition

sections.title: Artifact families
paragraphs: Disk artifacts can include file-system metadata, logs, configuration, application data, and deleted-file references. Memory can reveal running processes, loaded code, connections, and transient credentials, making handling particularly sensitive. Network artifacts show communications and metadata from selected observation points.

Cloud and software services add audit, identity, control-plane, application, and provider records with varying retention and export methods. No artifact is complete. Corroborate across independent sources and understand how collection, caching, clock behavior, and rotation affect each one.
keyPoints: Different artifacts answer different questions
Memory is volatile and highly sensitive
Corroboration reduces dependence on one imperfect source
sections.analogy: A trip can be reconstructed from tickets, maps, receipts, photos, and messages, each showing only part of the journey.
howTo: Map each forensic question to artifact types
Record conflicts instead of hiding them

sections.title: Timeline and reporting
paragraphs: A forensic timeline normalizes timestamps while preserving original values, zones, source, precision, and meaning. File creation time, log event time, collection time, and analyst action time are not interchangeable. Clock drift and automated updates can create misleading sequences.

Reports distinguish observed fact from interpretation, explain methods, preserve reproducibility, describe limitations, and use calibrated confidence. In labs, use synthetic disk or memory images. Never acquire or analyze a real person's device or memory without explicit authority and appropriate handling.
keyPoints: Timestamp semantics matter
Reports separate fact, inference, and limitation
Forensic access is explicit and purpose-bound
sections.analogy: A historian preserves original dates and calendars before placing records on one shared timeline.
howTo: Peer review methods and conclusion language

callout.text: Training images are safe practice material; production evidence may require legal, privacy, human-resources, or specialist involvement.

workflow: Confirm authority, objectives, scope, and handling requirements
Prioritize sources by volatility, value, safety, and availability
Acquire, label, hash, and secure evidence with chain of custody
Analyze verified copies and correlate artifacts
Report facts, methods, limitations, confidence, and disposition

commands.title: Verify a synthetic evidence image hash
commands.explanation: This lab command checks a supplied synthetic image against its supplied SHA-256 digest; it does not acquire memory.

quiz.question: Why consider order of volatility?
options: Transient evidence may disappear before durable evidence
It authorizes collection from any system
quiz.explanation: Collection planning gives early attention to valuable state likely to be lost.

quiz.question: What does matching a cryptographic hash demonstrate?
options: The compared bytes have not changed with overwhelming practical confidence
quiz.explanation: A hash supports integrity comparison but not provenance, relevance, authorization, or truthfulness.

quiz.question: What belongs in chain-of-custody records?
options: Collection, authority, handlers, methods, integrity, storage, transfers, and disposition
quiz.explanation: Complete handling records help establish control and reproducibility throughout evidence life.

quiz.question: Which reporting practice is strongest?
options: Explain methods and separate observations, interpretations, confidence, and limitations
quiz.explanation: Transparent methods and calibrated claims make findings reviewable and defensible.

practice.title: Plan evidence collection for a fictional server
practice.brief: A synthetic application server may have executed an unauthorized tool. It is still running and supports a noncritical training service.
tasks: Define authority, questions, and scope
Rank volatile and durable evidence
Draft acquisition and chain-of-custody records
Identify disk, memory, network, and service artifacts
Outline a source-aware timeline and report
answerGuide: The plan confirms incident authority, privacy boundaries, and intended questions
Memory, processes, and connections are considered before more durable sources with impact tradeoffs
Identifiers, collector, time, tool, hash, storage, access, and transfer are documented
Artifacts are selected for questions rather than collected indiscriminately
Original timestamps, facts, inferences, conflicts, confidence, and limitations remain visible
practice.safety: Plan against the fictional system and use only supplied synthetic evidence; do not acquire from a live device.

title: Safe Malware Analysis Concepts
summary: Understand safe static and dynamic analysis, file identity, portable executable concepts, behavior, and YARA-style pattern matching without handling live malware.
roleConnection: Malware analysis supports incident scoping and detection when performed by trained personnel in isolated, authorized environments with careful evidence handling.
objectives: Distinguish static analysis from controlled dynamic analysis
Explain hashes, strings, and Portable Executable structure at a conceptual level
Describe behavioral observations and the purpose of YARA
Design an isolated lab safety plan without obtaining or executing live malware
jdResponsibilities: Analyze suspicious files and behavior in authorized isolated environments
Extract defensive indicators and behavior for incident scoping
Develop safe pattern-matching concepts for malware identification
Communicate malware findings and handling risk

sections.title: Purpose, authorization, and triage
paragraphs: Malware is software or code used to cause unauthorized harm. Analysis asks defensive questions: what kind of file is this, what behavior was observed, which systems may be affected, and what evidence can improve containment or detection? It does not require discovering every capability.

Treat an unknown file as hazardous. Confirm business need, authority, provenance, hash, storage, handling rules, and qualified analysts. This course uses descriptions and inert text only; it provides no malware sample, exploit payload, credential-theft method, persistence instruction, or operational evasion guidance.
keyPoints: Analysis starts with defensive questions
Unknown files require hazardous-material discipline
The curriculum does not provide live or weaponized content
sections.analogy: A hazardous-material team identifies a substance in a controlled lab rather than opening it at an office desk.
howTo: Decide whether specialist analysis is necessary
Keep untrusted files out of ordinary environments

callout.text: Never download or execute live malware for this curriculum.

sections.title: Static analysis concepts
paragraphs: Static analysis examines a file without running it. Basic properties include cryptographic hashes, size, type, metadata, readable strings, signatures, and structural features. A hash identifies exact bytes for comparison but changes after any byte change and does not establish intent.

Strings may reveal library names, paths, messages, or configuration, but they can be unused, encoded, or deliberately misleading. Metadata can be forged. Combine observations and label hypotheses rather than treating one suspicious word as proof.
keyPoints: Static analysis avoids execution
Hashes identify exact content, not behavior
Strings and metadata require corroboration
sections.analogy: Inspecting a sealed product's label, weight, and packaging gives clues without operating it.
howTo: Use only an approved inert training file

sections.title: PE and behavior concepts
paragraphs: Portable Executable, or PE, is a Windows file format used by executables and libraries. Conceptually it contains headers and sections describing code, data, imports, resources, and loading needs. Odd structure can be a lead but legitimate packers and unusual compilers exist.

Dynamic analysis observes execution in a controlled environment: processes, files, configuration changes, network attempts, and system interactions. Observation is not permission to let a sample reach real services. Specialists use instrumentation, known snapshots, and strict containment.
keyPoints: PE structure helps organize static observations
Structural oddity is not verdict
Dynamic analysis must be isolated and controlled
sections.analogy: A blueprint describes rooms and utilities; observing an empty test building shows how those systems operate.
howTo: Learn PE structure from benign training files
Use supplied behavior reports rather than executing malware
Escalate live analysis to an approved specialist lab

sections.title: YARA concept and defensive outputs
paragraphs: YARA is a pattern-matching tool whose rules combine metadata, string or byte patterns, and a condition. Good rules select stable, distinctive features and avoid generic strings that match common software. Rule quality is tested against known positive and diverse benign files.

Defensive outputs may include exact hashes, higher-level behaviors, filenames with context, paths, domains, certificates, mutex-like artifacts, detection ideas, and collection gaps. Each output needs provenance, confidence, likely lifetime, and sharing classification.
keyPoints: YARA expresses pattern conditions
Distinctive stable features reduce false positives
Outputs need context, confidence, and lifecycle
sections.analogy: A field guide identifies a plant using a combination of leaf shape, stem, habitat, and flower rather than color alone.
howTo: Add a condition requiring a combination

sections.title: Isolated lab safety
paragraphs: A specialist malware lab separates analysis systems from production identities, data, networks, shared storage, and management planes. It uses controlled transfer, restricted or simulated networking, snapshots, monitoring, secure evidence storage, and a reset process. Isolation claims must be tested.

A personal Virtual Machine is not automatically safe: clipboard, shared folders, host integration, networking, and reused credentials can bridge boundaries. In production, follow the designated analysis service and incident process. In this course, limit practice to inert strings and published documentation.
keyPoints: Isolation covers identity, data, network, and management paths
Convenience integrations can break containment
Live analysis belongs to trained authorized specialists
sections.analogy: A biological clean room controls doors, air, equipment, waste, clothing, and decontamination, not just the workbench.
howTo: Have a qualified owner validate containment

callout.text: The safest beginner malware lab contains no live malware.

workflow: Confirm defensive need, authority, handling, and specialist ownership
Identify and preserve the item without execution
Perform approved static review or use a supplied behavior report
Correlate defensive observations with incident evidence
Share contextualized findings and securely retain or dispose under policy

commands.title: Inert YARA rule structure
commands.code:
rule Training_Text_Only {
  strings:
    $a = "fictional training marker alpha"
    $b = "fictional training marker beta"
  condition:
    all of them
}
commands.explanation: This non-operational text illustrates rule structure using harmless fictional phrases and is not a malware signature.

quiz.question: What is static analysis?
options: Examining file properties without executing it
Running an unknown file on a work laptop
Allowing a sample unrestricted internet access
quiz.explanation: Static analysis inspects content and structure without launching the file.

quiz.question: What does a file hash establish?
options: A practical identifier for exact bytes, not intent
quiz.explanation: Hashes support matching and integrity but cannot determine behavior or trustworthiness alone.

quiz.question: Why test a YARA concept against benign files?
options: To identify overly broad patterns and false positives
quiz.explanation: Negative testing shows whether supposedly distinctive conditions also match legitimate material.

quiz.question: What is appropriate beginner practice?
options: Reuse production credentials in a VM
Use inert text, benign files, and supplied reports
quiz.explanation: Concepts can be learned without creating execution or handling risk.

practice.title: Analyze an inert fictional file report
practice.brief: A supplied text report describes a harmless training file's hash, PE-like sections, strings, signer state, and simulated process and network observations.
tasks: Separate static from dynamic observations
Explain what the hash can and cannot establish
Identify three hypotheses and needed corroboration
Draft an inert YARA-style pattern concept
Write handling and escalation recommendations
answerGuide: File structure and strings are static while process and network records are reported dynamic evidence
The digest identifies exact bytes but not origin, safety, or behavior
Hypotheses remain qualified and connect to endpoint and network evidence
The pattern combines distinctive fictional text and is tested against benign text
No execution is proposed; live work is routed to authorized specialists
practice.safety: The exercise contains no live malware. Do not seek samples or convert the inert rule into an operational signature without review.

title: Risk-Based Vulnerability Management
summary: Manage vulnerabilities from discovery and validation through contextual prioritization, ownership, remediation, exception, verification, and metrics.
roleConnection: Vulnerability management connects technical weaknesses to accountable service decisions and verifies durable risk reduction rather than merely publishing scan counts.
objectives: Explain discovery and validation limits
Combine Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), exploit evidence, exposure, and business context
Manage remediation and time-bounded exceptions through ownership
Verify outcomes and select meaningful program metrics
jdResponsibilities: Operate vulnerability identification, prioritization, and remediation processes
Analyze scanner findings, CVSS, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (CISA KEV), exposure, and asset criticality
Coordinate vulnerability owners, exceptions, vendors, and remediation timelines
Report vulnerability risk, progress, verification, and program metrics

sections.title: Discovery and validation
paragraphs: Vulnerabilities can be discovered through authenticated and unauthenticated scanning, asset and software inventory, code analysis, dependency records, cloud posture tools, vendor advisories, penetration tests, incident findings, and researcher reports. Every method has coverage and accuracy limits.

Validation confirms that the asset, software, version, configuration, exposure, and finding apply. Scanner output can be stale, duplicated, credential-limited, or based on banners. Do not run scans outside approved scope; even routine scanning can affect fragile systems or breach agreements.
keyPoints: Use several discovery sources
A finding requires asset and applicability validation
Scanning is an authorized production activity
sections.analogy: A medical screening identifies cases needing review; it is not the final diagnosis.
howTo: Resolve finding to current asset and software

callout.text: Never scan systems, applications, or suppliers without explicit authorization and a safety plan.

sections.title: CVSS, context, and KEV
paragraphs: The Common Vulnerability Scoring System, or CVSS, describes technical severity characteristics. It is useful input but not an organization's complete risk score. Internet exposure, privileges, exploit prerequisites, data and safety impact, reachable paths, existing controls, and recovery options shape local priority.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, or CISA KEV, records vulnerabilities known to be exploited and adds a strong urgency signal. Absence from KEV does not prove no exploitation, and inclusion still requires asset applicability and coordinated action.
keyPoints: CVSS is technical severity, not complete business risk
CISA KEV is evidence of known exploitation
Local exposure and consequence affect priority
sections.analogy: A storm category describes the storm, while evacuation priority also depends on location, building strength, and vulnerable residents.
howTo: Check KEV and credible exploit evidence
Assess operational, data, and safety consequence

sections.title: Ownership and remediation choices
paragraphs: Assign an accountable service owner and a technical remediation owner. Options include patching, upgrading, changing configuration, removing software, restricting exposure, adding a compensating control, replacing a component, or accepting time-bounded residual risk through governance.

The technically fastest change may not be the safest. Dependencies, testing, maintenance windows, vendor support, rollback, resilience, and operational technology constraints matter. Emergency action still needs authority and validation.
keyPoints: Accountability includes service and technical ownership
Remediation is broader than patching
Operational constraints shape safe timing and method
sections.analogy: Repairing a bridge requires both the transport authority's decision and engineers who plan the safe work.
howTo: Notify the verified owner with evidence
Plan test, change, validation, monitoring, and rollback

sections.title: Exceptions and verification
paragraphs: An exception documents why the expected treatment cannot occur on time, the residual risk, affected assets, compensating controls, accountable acceptance, monitoring, expiry, and a future plan. It is not a silent status label or permanent waiver.

Verification checks the intended risk reduction after change. Rescan when safe, inspect version and configuration, validate exposure and controls, and watch for regression. A closed ticket without technical evidence does not prove the weakness is resolved.
keyPoints: Exceptions are explicit, owned, monitored, and temporary
Verification tests the actual outcome
Closure evidence should match the vulnerability condition
sections.analogy: A temporary building-code variance states limits, safeguards, approver, expiry, and a path to compliance.
howTo: Verify remediation or renew through governance

sections.title: Metrics and program improvement
paragraphs: Useful metrics answer risk and process questions: coverage of managed assets, validated backlog by priority and age, remediation time distributions, overdue high-risk items, exception age, recurrence, verification rate, and ownership gaps. Averages alone can hide a dangerous tail.

Avoid rewarding superficial closure or comparing teams without context. Report definitions, exclusions, data quality, trends, and denominators. In labs, prioritize synthetic findings. Production scanner, patch, firewall, or exception changes follow authorized ownership and change processes.
keyPoints: Metrics should drive decisions, not cosmetic closure
Distributions and aging reveal hidden risk
Definitions and coverage make numbers interpretable
sections.analogy: A hospital tracks wait-time distributions and outcomes, not just the number of patients discharged.
howTo: Name the decision each metric supports

callout.text: This prioritization model is general education and does not describe any specific employer's internal process.

workflow: Discover findings within authorized scope
Validate asset, applicability, exposure, and evidence
Prioritize using severity, exploitation, controls, and consequence
Assign owners to remediate or govern a time-bounded exception
Verify risk reduction and improve coverage and metrics

quiz.question: Why validate a scanner finding?
options: The asset, version, configuration, or evidence may be stale or inapplicable
quiz.explanation: Validation confirms that the reported condition applies to the current owned asset.

quiz.question: What does CVSS primarily describe?
quiz.explanation: Local exposure, controls, exploitation, and consequences must supplement CVSS.

quiz.question: What is a sound vulnerability exception?
options: Time-bounded risk acceptance with owner, safeguards, monitoring, and plan
A scanner suppression with no review
quiz.explanation: An exception governs residual risk transparently and returns for review.

quiz.question: What verifies remediation?
options: A team said work probably completed
Technical evidence shows the vulnerable condition or exposure was removed or controlled
quiz.explanation: Outcome-based verification checks the condition that created risk, not administrative status alone.

practice.title: Prioritize a fictional vulnerability backlog
practice.brief: A synthetic list includes an internet service in CISA KEV, a high-CVSS isolated lab server, an unsupported internal appliance, and duplicate workstation findings.
tasks: Validate asset, owner, version, exposure, and duplicates
Rank findings using CVSS, KEV, controls, and impact
Choose remediation options and safe change needs
Draft an exception for the unsupported appliance
Select verification evidence and four metrics
answerGuide: Uncertain inventory and applicability are resolved before ranking
Known exploitation and exposed critical service can outrank a higher score with low exposure
Options account for dependencies, vendor support, testing, monitoring, and rollback
The exception names residual risk, compensating controls, approver, monitoring, expiry, and replacement plan
Verification tests conditions; metrics include coverage, age, priority, time, exceptions, and verification
practice.safety: Use only the synthetic backlog. Do not scan, patch, or expose a real system.

title: Application and Application Programming Interface Security
summary: Integrate threat modeling, secure design, identity, validation, testing, and operations across the Software Development Lifecycle.
roleConnection: Application security practitioners help product teams prevent defects early, validate controls safely, and respond to application risk without becoming a release gate disconnected from business context.
objectives: Place security activities throughout the Software Development Lifecycle
Build a simple threat model using assets, trust boundaries, and abuse cases
Explain common Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) web and Application Programming Interface risk categories
Distinguish authentication, session, input, output, and authorized testing controls
jdResponsibilities: Perform application security reviews and threat modeling
Advise development teams on secure design and coding controls
Coordinate authorized security testing and remediation
Assess web, API, authentication, session, input, and output risks

sections.title: Security across the SDLC
paragraphs: The Software Development Lifecycle, or SDLC, covers planning, requirements, design, implementation, testing, release, operation, and retirement. Security at each stage is cheaper and more reliable than one final test: define abuse resistance, review architecture, protect dependencies, test controls, monitor behavior, and retire data safely.

Product teams own delivery and risk decisions with appropriate governance; security supplies expertise, patterns, review, and evidence. Tailor depth to data sensitivity, exposure, criticality, change rate, and consequence instead of imposing identical ceremony on every application.
keyPoints: Security belongs throughout the SDLC
Early design choices prevent classes of defects
Assurance should be proportionate to risk
sections.analogy: Building safety includes requirements, blueprints, materials, inspections, occupancy, maintenance, and demolition, not one check before opening.

sections.title: Threat modeling
paragraphs: Threat modeling is structured reasoning about what is being built, what can go wrong, what safeguards exist, and whether they are sufficient. A data-flow diagram identifies actors, processes, stores, flows, and trust boundaries; abuse cases describe how an objective could be harmed.

Use models to drive decisions, not to decorate documents. Include architects, developers, operators, business and data owners, and security. Record assumptions, unresolved questions, controls, owners, and validation so the model changes with the system.
keyPoints: Model the actual design and data flow
Abuse cases connect threats to business impact
Threat models need owners and maintenance
sections.analogy: A stage crew rehearses what happens if power, sound, access, or crowd flow fails before opening night.
howTo: Draw actors, components, data, and trust boundaries
Validate and update after design changes

sections.title: Web and API risk categories
paragraphs: OWASP publishes awareness material about broad risks such as broken access control, cryptographic failures, injection, insecure design, security misconfiguration, vulnerable components, authentication failures, integrity failures, logging failures, and server-side request forgery. Categories guide questions rather than prove a defect.

An Application Programming Interface, or API, exposes operations to software clients. API risks often involve object- and function-level authorization, resource consumption, inventory, unsafe third-party consumption, and configuration. Every request should be authorized for the actor, action, and object.
keyPoints: OWASP categories organize review
APIs require object and function authorization
Inventory and lifecycle reduce forgotten exposure
sections.analogy: A hotel front desk verifies not just that a guest exists, but that the guest may access this room and request this service.
howTo: Set resource limits and schema expectations

sections.title: Identity, sessions, input, and output
paragraphs: Authentication verifies identity; session management maintains authenticated state; authorization checks each protected action. Sessions need secure identifiers, expiration, revocation, transport protection, and resistance to reuse. Reauthentication may be appropriate for high-risk actions.

Validate input against expected type, length, range, structure, and business rules. Parameterized interfaces keep data separate from commands. Context-aware output encoding reduces injection into browsers or other consumers. Validation and encoding solve different problems and both can be necessary.
keyPoints: Authenticate, manage session, then authorize every action
Input validation uses positive expectations
Output encoding depends on the destination context
sections.analogy: An event ticket is checked at entry, remains valid for a limited event, and is checked again for restricted backstage areas.
howTo: Set session creation, expiry, and revocation
Authorize server-side on every sensitive operation

sections.title: Security testing and boundaries
paragraphs: Assurance can include code review, dependency analysis, static analysis, dynamic testing, configuration review, unit and integration security tests, and authorized penetration testing. Tools find different defect classes and produce false positives and negatives, so results need validation and risk context.

Practice only in intentionally vulnerable labs such as authorized learning platforms or applications you own and isolate. Never test an employer, internet target, supplier, or production application without written scope and coordination. Production fixes require owner review, regression testing, monitoring, and rollback.
keyPoints: Combine complementary assurance methods
Testing requires explicit scope and safe conditions
Fixes can create functional and security regression
sections.analogy: Vehicle safety uses design standards, component tests, crash tests, inspections, and recalls under controlled conditions.
howTo: Validate and report without unnecessary sensitive detail

callout.text: A public website is not an invitation to test it. Use only owned or explicitly authorized labs.

workflow: Classify the application, data, exposure, and owners
Define security and privacy requirements
Threat model design and select controls
Implement and test with authorized complementary methods
Release, monitor, remediate, and retire through controlled processes

quiz.question: When should application security begin?
options: During planning and requirements, then continue through retirement
quiz.explanation: Security decisions and evidence belong across the full SDLC.

quiz.question: What does a threat model primarily support?
options: Structured decisions about assets, abuse cases, trust boundaries, and controls
quiz.explanation: Threat modeling makes design risk and control decisions explicit and reviewable.

quiz.question: Which authorization question should an API answer?
options: Is the request formatted as JSON only?
May this actor perform this action on this object?
Does the client know the route name?
quiz.explanation: Authentication alone is insufficient; protected operations need object- and function-level authorization.

quiz.question: Where should a beginner practice web security testing?
options: A production service during quiet hours
An intentionally vulnerable lab they are authorized to use
quiz.explanation: Testing can cause harm and is appropriate only within explicit scope such as purpose-built labs.

practice.title: Threat model a fictional expense API
practice.brief: A synthetic mobile app submits expenses to an API that stores receipts, calls an identity provider, and sends approved payments to a finance service.
tasks: Draw actors, components, data flows, and trust boundaries
Write five abuse cases across OWASP categories
Define authentication, session, and authorization controls
Define input, output, logging, and resource controls
Plan safe assurance and remediation
answerGuide: The model includes employee, approver, API, identity, receipt store, finance service, and administrative paths
Abuse cases connect actor, action, object, data, and business impact
Server-side object and function authorization follows least privilege
Schemas, file limits, safe rendering, secrets, rate controls, and useful logs are present
Testing uses synthetic data and approved labs, while fixes use regression, monitoring, and rollback
practice.safety: Keep the scenario fictional and perform no testing against a live application or API.

title: Cloud Security Across Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud
summary: Apply shared responsibility, identity, network, encryption, secrets, logging, posture, and incident-response principles across major cloud service models.
roleConnection: Cloud security practitioners connect provider controls with customer configuration and operating responsibilities while preserving evidence across identities, resources, and control planes.
objectives: Apply shared responsibility across infrastructure, platform, and software services
Design least-privilege cloud identities and network paths
Explain cloud encryption, key, and secrets responsibilities
Plan logging, posture management, and cloud incident response across Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud
jdResponsibilities: Assess and improve cloud security architecture and posture
Review cloud identity, network, encryption, secrets, and logging controls
Support cloud incident detection, response, and recovery
Collaborate across Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, platform, application, and vendor teams

sections.title: Shared responsibility
paragraphs: Shared responsibility divides security work between a cloud provider and customer. The provider generally secures underlying facilities and service infrastructure; the customer remains responsible for data, identities, configurations, workloads, and use to degrees that vary by service model.

Infrastructure as a Service leaves more operating responsibility with the customer than Platform as a Service, while Software as a Service shifts more stack operation to the provider. Responsibility never disappears: customers still govern access, data, configuration, integration, monitoring, and supplier assurance.
keyPoints: Responsibility varies by service and configuration
The provider and customer both have duties
Managed service does not mean unmanaged risk
sections.analogy: Renting a building shifts structural maintenance to the landlord, but the tenant still controls occupants, valuables, and daily operations.
howTo: List provider, customer, and shared tasks
Define evidence that each responsibility operates

sections.title: Cloud IAM
paragraphs: Cloud Identity and Access Management, or IAM, controls human and workload identities, roles, policies, trust, and credentials. Prefer centralized lifecycle, strong authentication, short-lived credentials, narrow roles, workload identity, separation of duties, and emergency access with monitoring.

AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud use different names and policy models. The durable questions are the same: who or what is acting, how was it authenticated, what policy allowed the action, on which resource, under what conditions, and who reviews the access?
keyPoints: Human and workload identities need separate lifecycle controls
Short-lived scoped access reduces credential risk
Effective permission can combine many policies
sections.analogy: A campus badge system has students, staff, service contractors, room schedules, emergency keys, and reviewable access rules.
howTo: Inventory identity types and trust paths
Remove standing broad privilege where feasible

sections.title: Network, encryption, and secrets
paragraphs: Cloud network controls include virtual networks, subnets, routing, security groups or rules, gateways, private service paths, firewalls, load balancers, and name services. Public reachability can arise through several layers, so evaluate the effective path rather than one setting.

Encryption protects data in transit and at rest according to service design. Key management defines creation, access, rotation, recovery, and deletion responsibilities. Secrets such as API keys and tokens should use managed stores, workload identity where possible, limited scope, rotation, and access logging, not source code.
keyPoints: Evaluate effective cloud reachability
Key ownership and lifecycle matter to encryption
Secrets belong in managed systems, not code or logs
sections.analogy: A secure warehouse needs controlled roads and doors, locked containers, managed keys, and records of who retrieved each key.
howTo: Map ingress, egress, and private paths
Identify data states and encryption controls
Assign key administrators and users separately

sections.title: Logging and posture
paragraphs: Cloud evidence can include identity sign-ins, administrative control-plane actions, resource configuration changes, network flows, workload logs, data access, key use, and security-service findings. Enable appropriate logs early, route them to protected destinations, and monitor health, retention, cost, and access.

Cloud Security Posture Management, or CSPM, compares resources with policies and risk patterns. Findings need validation, ownership, priority, and safe remediation just like vulnerabilities. Multicloud normalization helps scale but must preserve provider-specific meaning.
keyPoints: Control-plane and identity logs are central evidence
Logs need protected independent retention
Posture findings require context and workflow
sections.analogy: A property manager combines master-key records, building permits, door alarms, utility readings, and tenant reports.
howTo: Protect log destinations from workload administrators
Validate posture findings against service context

sections.title: Cloud incident response and safe change
paragraphs: Cloud incidents can cross identity, control plane, data plane, software pipeline, managed service, and provider responsibility. Preparation includes account and project contacts, evidence export, emergency roles, snapshots, key and session actions, provider escalation, communications, and recovery patterns.

A console makes powerful changes easy, not automatically safe. In labs, use disposable accounts with budgets and synthetic data. In production, policy, identity, network, key, logging, and resource changes require owner authorization, infrastructure-as-code review where applicable, validation, monitoring, and rollback.
keyPoints: Cloud incidents cross several planes
Provider escalation can be part of response
Console convenience does not remove change risk
sections.analogy: A high-rise incident plan coordinates tenants, building management, utilities, emergency services, and access systems.
howTo: Identify affected tenant, account, subscription, project, region, and resource
Assess sessions, keys, data, and infrastructure changes
Coordinate authorized containment with provider and owners
Recover from trusted definitions and monitor

callout.text: Provider terms here are public/general. No cloud provider, architecture, or process is attributed to ExxonMobil or another employer.

workflow: Classify cloud service and shared responsibilities
Map identities, data, networks, keys, secrets, logs, and owners
Assess posture and threats across control and data planes
Implement through reviewed configuration or code with validation
Monitor health and prepare evidence, containment, recovery, and provider escalation

quiz.question: What happens to customer security responsibility when using Software as a Service?
options: It changes but still includes access, data, configuration, integration, and governance
quiz.explanation: The provider operates more of the stack, while customers retain important usage and governance responsibilities.

quiz.question: What is preferred for a cloud workload needing service access?
options: A shared human password in source code
A scoped workload identity with short-lived credentials
quiz.explanation: Workload identity and short-lived scoped access improve attribution and reduce secret exposure.

quiz.question: Why protect cloud audit logs in a separate controlled destination?
options: To reduce the chance a compromised workload administrator can alter evidence
quiz.explanation: Independent access and retention help preserve trustworthy incident evidence.

quiz.question: How should a production CSPM finding be remediated?
options: Click the suggested change without review
Assume every service uses the same architecture
Validate context, assign an owner, test the change, monitor, and retain rollback
quiz.explanation: Automated guidance still requires service and operational context.

practice.title: Secure a fictional multicloud analytics service
practice.brief: A synthetic service receives data in AWS, processes it in Azure, and shares aggregated results with a Google Cloud project.
tasks: Create a shared-responsibility matrix
Map human and workload IAM
Map networks, encryption, keys, and secrets
Define control-plane, data, and workload logging
Plan posture review and one incident scenario
answerGuide: Each exact service has provider, customer, shared tasks, owners, and evidence
Roles are least-privileged with federation, workload identity, emergency access, and review
Effective public and private paths, data states, key lifecycle, and secret storage are shown
Logs are protected, health-monitored, retained, and correlated without erasing provider meaning
The plan includes validated findings, provider contacts, evidence, authorized containment, recovery, and rollback
practice.safety: Keep the design fictional. Do not create billable resources, modify a cloud tenant, or use real credentials.

title: Detection Engineering
summary: Engineer detections from risk and telemetry requirements through Sigma-style logic, testing, controlled deployment, monitoring, tuning, versioning, and retirement.
roleConnection: Detection engineers create dependable, reviewable monitoring content that turns observable behavior into actionable evidence without overwhelming responders or destabilizing production.
objectives: Define a detection use case, behavior, scope, and responder action
Specify telemetry and data-quality requirements
Explain Sigma concepts and translate logic carefully
Test, version, deploy, monitor, tune, roll back, and retire detections safely
jdResponsibilities: Design, build, test, and maintain security detections
Define telemetry requirements and improve monitoring coverage
Tune false positives while preserving detection intent
Manage production monitoring changes, version control, metrics, and rollback

sections.title: Use-case definition
paragraphs: A detection use case begins with risk and observable behavior, not a query copied from another environment. Define threat behavior, protected outcome, scope, expected entities, data, analytic approach, severity rationale, investigation evidence, responder action, owner, and limitations.

Map behavior to MITRE ATT&CK when evidence supports it, but write plain-language intent first. Decide whether the best result is a real-time alert, scheduled analytic, correlation, dashboard, hunt, or preventive control. Not every useful observation should wake a responder.
keyPoints: Detection intent precedes syntax
Use cases connect behavior to action
Alerting is one of several possible outputs
sections.analogy: A medical test is designed for a condition, population, evidence, and treatment decision before choosing laboratory equipment.

sections.title: Telemetry requirements
paragraphs: Specify required sources, event types, fields, values, timestamps, entity identifiers, enrichment, retention, latency, coverage, and health. A logically perfect analytic fails if a key field is absent or delayed. Optional fields and fallback logic should be explicit.

Evaluate privacy, volume, storage, performance, and ownership before requesting new telemetry. Validate representative raw events and transformations. Add data-health monitoring so loss or schema drift is visible rather than silently reducing coverage.
keyPoints: Data contracts support dependable detections
Telemetry has operational and privacy cost
Coverage includes pipeline-health visibility
sections.analogy: A recipe names ingredients and quality; it cannot succeed reliably when half the ingredients arrive unlabeled.
howTo: Map each condition to a source field
Define health alerts and source owner

sections.title: Sigma and portable logic
paragraphs: Sigma is a generic rule format for expressing log-source context, selections, conditions, and descriptive metadata. It can help share detection ideas across platforms. Backends translate rules, but field mappings, query semantics, case handling, time windows, and correlations vary.

A translated rule is a candidate, not proven production content. Validate it against the target schema and engine. Include title, identifier, status, description, references, authoring history, log source, logic, false-positive notes, level, tags, tests, and ownership as appropriate.
keyPoints: Sigma separates general intent from some platform syntax
Translation cannot solve unknown schema semantics
Metadata and tests are part of the detection
sections.analogy: A musical score is portable, but each orchestra still rehearses with its instruments and venue.
howTo: Map it to a validated log source
Compare generated logic with target semantics

sections.title: Testing and false positives
paragraphs: Test syntax, logic, field mapping, expected positive cases, near misses, known benign activity, missing data, volume, latency, and investigation output. Historical replay can estimate behavior but may not represent future populations or pipeline changes.

A false positive is an alert that matches logic but does not represent the intended risk. Tune by improving context, population, sequence, threshold, or enrichment rather than broadly excluding noisy entities. Track false negatives and untestable gaps as seriously as noise.
keyPoints: Testing includes positive, negative, edge, and operational cases
Broad allowlists can create blind spots
False-negative risk belongs in tuning decisions
sections.analogy: A metal detector is tested with prohibited items, harmless objects, unusual bags, crowds, and equipment failures.
howTo: Create synthetic positive and benign fixtures
Run logic in a non-alerting test mode
Record expected outcome and coverage gaps

sections.title: Production lifecycle and rollback
paragraphs: Store detection content, documentation, tests, and changes in version control. Peer review should cover intent, data, logic, privacy, performance, responder readiness, and rollback. Deploy progressively when possible and monitor query health, result volume, alert latency, responder feedback, and data drift.

Production monitoring changes can suppress real signals, expose sensitive data, increase cost, or flood a queue. Use authorized change processes, communicate impacts, preserve the previous version, and define rollback triggers. Retire content only after checking dependencies, coverage replacement, and evidence retention.
keyPoints: Detections are operated products
Safe deployment includes progressive monitoring and rollback
Retirement needs dependency and coverage review
sections.analogy: Air-traffic software changes are versioned, reviewed, staged, watched, and reversible because both silence and noise matter.
howTo: Deploy safely in monitor-only or limited scope
Watch health, quality, cost, and queue effects
Roll back or promote using predefined criteria

callout.text: Never disable, suppress, or deploy a production detection outside authorized change and incident processes.

workflow: Define risk, behavior, scope, evidence, and response
Validate telemetry, schema, coverage, health, and cost
Implement versioned logic and investigation context
Test positive, benign, edge, performance, and failure cases
Review, deploy progressively, monitor, tune, roll back, and retire

commands.title: Harmless Sigma training rule
commands.code:
