status: test
logsource:
  product: training
detection:
  selection:
    event_type: synthetic_admin_action
    outcome: failure
  condition: selection
level: low
commands.explanation: This test-only rule illustrates Sigma structure against a fictional log source and is not ready for any production backend.

quiz.question: What should come first in detection engineering?
options: A defined risk behavior, evidence, scope, and responder decision
quiz.explanation: Intent and actionability guide telemetry, implementation, tests, and operations.

quiz.question: Why monitor telemetry health?
options: A detection may silently lose coverage when sources or schemas fail
Health proves every event is malicious
quiz.explanation: Detection logic depends on timely, correctly parsed, sufficiently complete data.

quiz.question: What is true of a translated Sigma rule?
options: It is automatically safe for production
It still requires target-schema, semantic, test, and performance validation
quiz.explanation: Backends cannot infer all local data and engine behavior.

quiz.question: What is the safest response to alert noise?
options: Analyze causes and tune context while testing for lost coverage and keeping rollback
quiz.explanation: Controlled tuning balances responder burden with missed-detection risk.

practice.title: Engineer a synthetic admin-failure detection
practice.brief: A fictional application logs administrative actions with actor, target, outcome, source device, request identifier, and event time.
tasks: Define behavior, population, severity, and response
Write the telemetry contract and health checks
Draft Sigma-style logic and metadata
Design positive, benign, edge, and missing-data tests
Plan review, staged deployment, monitoring, and rollback
answerGuide: The use case explains why repeated or unusual failures matter and what responders decide
Required fields, clocks, identity, coverage, retention, privacy, and owners are specified
Logic is minimal, test-status, and tied to a fictional source
Tests include known administration, bursts, one-offs, absent fields, volume, and investigation context
Production-like steps preserve versions, require approval, watch queue and coverage, and define rollback
practice.safety: Use synthetic events and test status only. Do not deploy or modify any production monitoring content.

title: Safe Security Automation with Python and PowerShell
summary: Use beginner Python and PowerShell to parse JavaScript Object Notation (JSON), Comma-Separated Values (CSV), and logs, understand Application Programming Interface (API) concepts, validate inputs, handle errors, and protect secrets in read-only workflows.
roleConnection: Small, reviewed automations reduce repetitive analysis and improve consistency when they preserve evidence, fail safely, expose assumptions, and begin read-only.
objectives: Parse synthetic JSON, CSV, and line-oriented logs with Python and PowerShell
Explain Application Programming Interface requests, responses, pagination, and limits
Validate inputs and handle partial failure safely
Keep credentials and secrets out of code, logs, and shared output
jdResponsibilities: Automate repetitive security analysis and reporting tasks
Integrate security data through APIs and structured files
Build validation, error handling, auditability, and safe defaults
Protect automation secrets and coordinate reviewed production changes

sections.title: Choose the right automation
paragraphs: Automate stable, understood, repeatable steps with clear inputs and outputs. Start by documenting the manual process and failure modes. A script that accelerates an incorrect or unowned process increases risk more efficiently.

Begin read-only with synthetic data. Define who owns the script, where it runs, permissions, dependencies, expected volume, logs, tests, review, recovery, and retirement. Human approval should remain where context, safety, or material business impact demands judgment.
keyPoints: Understand before automating
Read-only and synthetic are safe starting points
Automation needs ownership and lifecycle
sections.analogy: A conveyor belt helps only after the assembly steps and quality checks are understood.
howTo: Identify inputs, outputs, and failure effects

sections.title: JSON, CSV, and logs
paragraphs: JavaScript Object Notation, or JSON, represents objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. Comma-Separated Values, or CSV, represents rows and columns but requires careful quoting, delimiter, encoding, and header handling. Logs may be structured or free text.

Use parsers rather than splitting structured formats by hand. Validate expected type, required fields, value ranges, encoding, size, and duplicate behavior. Preserve the source record or reference so transformed output can be traced and corrected.
keyPoints: Use format-aware parsers
Parsing success does not prove semantic validity
Preserve traceability to input
sections.analogy: A translator can read grammar correctly while still needing context to know whether a sentence makes sense.
howTo: Decode with an explicit parser and encoding
Handle missing or extra values deliberately
Write deterministic output with source references

sections.title: Python and PowerShell patterns
paragraphs: Python offers standard modules such as json, csv, pathlib, and logging. PowerShell passes objects through a pipeline and includes commands such as ConvertFrom-Json, Import-Csv, Where-Object, and Select-Object. Both can build transparent read-only transformations.

Prefer clear names, small functions, explicit parameters, and predictable output over compressed one-liners. Pin and review dependencies where used, but standard libraries often suffice for beginner parsing. Never execute text taken from data as code.
keyPoints: Both languages support object-oriented parsing workflows
Readable code improves review
Data must not become executable code
sections.analogy: A well-labeled workshop is safer to inspect and repair than a clever machine with hidden controls.
howTo: Write output without changing the input

sections.title: API and secrets concepts
paragraphs: An Application Programming Interface, or API, defines how software requests operations or data and receives status, headers, and a body. Clients must handle authentication, authorization, pagination, rate limits, timeouts, retries, versioning, and partial responses.

Secrets do not belong in source code, command history, screenshots, test fixtures, or logs. Use an approved secret store or workload identity, request minimum scope, avoid echoing tokens, rotate safely, and revoke when no longer needed. A masked secret can still leak through debug output.
keyPoints: API clients handle more than a successful response
Retries must avoid duplicate harmful actions
Secrets need managed storage and least scope
sections.analogy: An API is a service counter with a menu, ticket, queue limits, receipts, and rules; the access badge is not written on the order form.
howTo: Load secrets from an approved source without logging

sections.title: Validation, errors, and production safety
paragraphs: Fail safely: distinguish invalid input, unavailable dependency, permission denial, rate limit, and unexpected response. Do not silently skip errors and publish an incomplete total. Report processed, rejected, failed, and remaining records with machine-readable logs and a clear exit status.

A production automation that writes, isolates, blocks, deletes, or changes access requires stronger design: dry run, idempotency, approval, scoped blast radius, concurrency limits, audit records, monitoring, stop controls, rollback or compensation, and incident handling. Classroom examples remain read-only.
keyPoints: Errors should be classified and visible
Partial success must not masquerade as complete
Write automation requires explicit safeguards and authority
sections.analogy: A bank reconciliation reports unmatched transactions instead of dropping them to make totals balance.
howTo: Catch only errors you can handle
Return a failure status for incomplete output
Require review before any production or write capability

callout.text: Do not add production write actions, real tokens, or real employer data to these exercises.

workflow: Define and manually validate the repetitive task
Design least-privilege read-only inputs, outputs, and failure behavior
Implement clear parsing, validation, errors, and audit output
Test synthetic normal, edge, invalid, and dependency-failure cases
Review, run in controlled scope, monitor, and maintain or retire

commands.title: Summarize synthetic JSON in Python
commands.explanation: This read-only example validates the top-level type and summarizes a supplied synthetic file without credentials or network access.

commands.title: Summarize synthetic CSV in PowerShell
commands.code:
$rows = Import-Csv .\synthetic-events.csv
$rows | Group-Object outcome | Select-Object Name, Count | Sort-Object Count -Descending
commands.explanation: This read-only pipeline uses the CSV parser and returns grouped fictional outcomes.

quiz.question: What is a good first automation target?
options: A stable, understood, repetitive, read-only transformation
quiz.explanation: Low-impact, understood tasks let teams establish validation and operating discipline safely.

quiz.question: Why use a JSON or CSV parser instead of splitting strings manually?
options: They correctly handle format structure, quoting, and escaping
quiz.explanation: Format parsers handle syntax, while the script must still validate types and meaning.

quiz.question: Where should an automation secret be stored?
options: In an approved secret store or replaced by workload identity
quiz.explanation: Managed identity and secret systems reduce exposure and support lifecycle controls.

quiz.question: How should a script report partial processing failure?
options: Expose processed and failed counts, preserve errors, and return an incomplete status
quiz.explanation: Consumers must know whether output is complete and which records require attention.

practice.title: Build a read-only synthetic log summarizer
practice.brief: A fictional folder contains small JSON and CSV exports with event time, source, severity, outcome, and record identifier.
tasks: Define input schema, size limits, output, and failure behavior
Parse and validate both formats
Summarize severity and outcome while preserving source references
Handle malformed, missing, duplicate, and empty input
Write a production-readiness review without enabling writes
answerGuide: The contract names types, required fields, limits, encoding, and completeness status
Format-aware parsers and semantic checks are separate
Output is deterministic and traceable to record identifiers
Rejected and duplicate records are explicit with nonzero incomplete status
Read-only scope, owner, secrets, dependencies, tests, monitoring, and review are addressed
practice.safety: Use only supplied synthetic files and placeholder configuration. Do not insert credentials, call live APIs, or process employer data.

title: Security Engineering and Operations
summary: Move security controls from requirements and threat models through design, implementation, validation, operation, vendor management, issue resolution, change, awareness, and stakeholder communication.
roleConnection: Security engineers and operators keep controls effective over time by joining sound design with service ownership, evidence, vendor coordination, maintenance, and clear risk communication.
objectives: Translate risk and threat models into testable control requirements
Plan control implementation, validation, and ongoing operation
Evaluate vendor capability and shared operational responsibilities
Resolve issues and communicate change, risk, awareness, and decisions to stakeholders
jdResponsibilities: Design, implement, validate, and operate security controls
Evaluate security technologies and coordinate vendors and service providers
Resolve security operational issues and manage controlled changes
Deliver security awareness, risk communication, and stakeholder collaboration

sections.title: From risk to requirements
paragraphs: A control requirement should trace to an asset, risk, threat model, obligation, or design principle. State the intended outcome, scope, assumptions, performance and availability needs, privacy constraints, evidence, owner, failure behavior, and acceptance criteria without prematurely naming a product.

Distinguish functional requirements from assurance requirements. A gateway may need to restrict flows; assurance also asks how rules are reviewed, changes authorized, health monitored, failures handled, logs protected, and effectiveness tested.
keyPoints: Requirements trace to risk and outcomes
Avoid choosing a product before defining the need
Assurance explains how confidence is maintained
sections.analogy: A buyer specifies safe transport capacity and braking performance before selecting a vehicle model.
howTo: Define users, environment, dependencies, and constraints
Write measurable behavior and failure handling

sections.title: Design, implementation, and validation
paragraphs: Control design covers architecture, trust, identity, data, integration, resilience, administration, monitoring, and lifecycle. Review normal operation, misuse, component failure, degraded modes, emergency access, recovery, and retirement. Threat modeling exposes assumptions before implementation hardens them.

Implementation should use controlled environments, least-privileged administration, peer review, baseline configuration, documented dependencies, and rollback. Validation tests intended allow and deny behavior, failure cases, performance, evidence, recovery, and owner acceptance.
keyPoints: Design includes operation and failure
Implementation protects administrative paths
Validation tests outcomes and negative cases
sections.analogy: An elevator is designed for capacity, access, alarms, power loss, rescue, maintenance, and inspection, not only upward travel.
howTo: Build in a representative nonproduction environment
Test positive, negative, degraded, and recovery cases

sections.title: Operate and resolve issues
paragraphs: Operational readiness includes service ownership, runbooks, health indicators, alerts, capacity, dependencies, support tiers, access review, backups, patching, certificate and license expiry, continuity, incident integration, metrics, and regular control-effectiveness review.

When an issue occurs, stabilize safely, preserve evidence, assess scope and impact, communicate status, diagnose contributing causes, implement an approved fix, validate recovery, and capture learning. A workaround needs risk, owner, monitoring, and expiration.
keyPoints: Controls are services with lifecycle needs
Health is different from security effectiveness
Workarounds require governance and expiry
sections.analogy: A sprinkler system needs inspection, water pressure, clear valves, tested alarms, maintenance, and incident procedures after installation.
howTo: Use the runbook and escalation path
Stabilize with the least harmful authorized action
Fix and verify through change control
Update design, runbook, monitoring, and risk records

sections.title: Vendors and technology evaluation
paragraphs: Evaluate technology against requirements using transparent scenarios and representative data. Consider architecture, integration, identity, security, privacy, resilience, evidence access, performance, accessibility, support, roadmap, licensing, portability, exit, and total operating cost.

Vendor demonstrations and claims are inputs, not validation. Clarify shared responsibilities, incident contacts, service levels, vulnerability handling, update practices, data locations, subcontractors, change notification, audit evidence, and secure termination. Avoid disclosing sensitive production details unnecessarily during evaluation.
keyPoints: Evaluate against requirements and evidence
Operating and exit costs matter
Supplier responsibilities and incident paths must be explicit
sections.analogy: Selecting a fire alarm considers building fit, maintenance, inspections, emergency support, replacement parts, and removal, not just a showroom demonstration.
howTo: Review supplier security and contracts with specialists
Plan implementation, support, renewal, and exit

sections.title: Change, awareness, and stakeholder trust
paragraphs: Security change succeeds when stakeholders understand purpose, impact, timing, actions, support, and rollback. Tailor communication: leaders need decision and risk; operators need procedures and signals; users need plain-language behavior; vendors need explicit responsibilities.

Awareness should connect role-specific decisions to realistic examples and a simple reporting path, not rely on fear or blame. Listen to operational expertise, record disagreements and accepted risk, and close the loop after changes. This course describes general practices and no employer's internal process.
keyPoints: Communication is part of control effectiveness
Awareness should be role-specific and actionable
Document decisions, dissent, and follow-up respectfully
sections.analogy: A successful building renovation gives executives cost choices, crews plans, occupants schedules, and everyone an issue-reporting route.

callout.text: Do not infer ExxonMobil's technologies, suppliers, architecture, policy, or operating model from these general practices.

workflow: Translate risk and threat models into owned testable requirements
Design architecture, administration, failure handling, evidence, and lifecycle
Evaluate or build, then validate in representative safe conditions
Deploy through approved change and operate health, support, and effectiveness
Resolve issues, communicate risk, educate stakeholders, and improve or retire

quiz.question: What is the strongest starting point for selecting a security product?
options: Testable outcome and assurance requirements traced to risk
A product already used elsewhere without context
quiz.explanation: Requirements create an evidence-based basis for architecture and product decisions.

quiz.question: How does assurance differ from control function?
options: Assurance establishes how operation and effectiveness are evidenced over time
quiz.explanation: Functional behavior states what the control does; assurance supports confidence that it continues to do so.

quiz.question: What should a technology proof of concept use?
options: Real secrets copied into a vendor environment
Representative synthetic scenarios tied to requirements and failure cases
quiz.explanation: Controlled representative testing creates useful evidence without unnecessary production exposure.

quiz.question: What makes security awareness more effective?
options: The same technical lecture for every role
Role-relevant decisions, realistic examples, and clear actions and support
quiz.explanation: People can apply awareness when it relates to their responsibilities and offers usable next steps.

practice.title: Design a fictional secure file-transfer control
practice.brief: A synthetic business needs to exchange restricted files with several suppliers and retire an unsupported transfer service.
tasks: Write outcome, functional, assurance, and lifecycle requirements
Threat model identities, data, administration, failures, and suppliers
Create a vendor evaluation and synthetic proof-of-concept plan
Define implementation, validation, operations, and issue response
Draft executive, operator, supplier, and user communications
answerGuide: Requirements trace to confidentiality, integrity, availability, compliance, evidence, and ownership
Threats include access, misdelivery, key and admin risk, outage, retention, and termination
Evaluation covers architecture, support, resilience, evidence, total cost, responsibilities, and exit with synthetic data
The plan includes positive and negative tests, change, monitoring, runbooks, rollback, and effectiveness review
Communications are audience-specific, invite feedback, and state decisions and support
practice.safety: Keep data, vendors, and architecture fictional. Do not contact suppliers or test a real transfer service.

title: Critical Infrastructure Career Readiness
summary: Prepare ethically for critical-infrastructure security by respecting Information Technology (IT), Operational Technology (OT), and Industrial Control System (ICS) distinctions, safety and availability, first-day discovery, structured learning plans, and a defensive capstone.
roleConnection: A new professional earns trust by listening, protecting safety, learning local authority and architecture, asking precise questions, communicating uncertainty, and making reversible evidence-based contributions.
objectives: Distinguish Information Technology from Operational Technology and Industrial Control System priorities
Apply a safety- and availability-first mindset without assuming internal company practices
Use professional ethics and effective first-day questions
Create five-week pre-start and 30/60/90-day plans and synthesize the curriculum in a capstone
jdResponsibilities: Support cybersecurity for critical infrastructure with safety and availability awareness
Collaborate ethically with IT, OT, engineering, operations, leadership, and suppliers
Learn organizational architecture, policy, authority, and incident processes without assumptions
Build a professional development plan and communicate a defensive capstone

sections.title: IT, OT, and ICS distinctions
paragraphs: Information Technology, or IT, primarily processes information for business services. Operational Technology, or OT, monitors or controls physical processes. An Industrial Control System, or ICS, is a class of OT used in industrial operations. Boundaries overlap, and actual definitions and ownership vary by organization.

OT can include controllers, sensors, actuators, supervisory systems, engineering workstations, safety systems, networks, historians, and vendor support paths. Physical process state, equipment lifecycle, deterministic timing, and specialist engineering knowledge shape security decisions.
keyPoints: OT affects physical processes
ICS is within the broader OT landscape
Architecture and ownership must be learned locally
sections.analogy: IT may manage the shipping schedule, while OT operates the conveyor and safety interlocks that move physical packages.
howTo: Ask whether a system observes or changes a physical process

sections.title: Safety and availability mindset
paragraphs: Confidentiality, integrity, and availability still matter in OT, but human safety, environmental protection, product quality, equipment protection, and reliable operation can dominate decisions. A security action that reboots, scans, blocks, patches, or isolates may change a physical process.

Use asset and process owners, engineering review, tested procedures, maintenance windows, known-good configurations, backups, manual fallbacks, monitoring, and recovery criteria. Passive observation can still create data and privacy obligations; active testing requires explicit specialist approval.
keyPoints: Cyber actions can have physical consequences
Process safety and engineering authority shape response
Active OT testing is specialist and authorization-bound
sections.analogy: Repairing an aircraft in flight is different from repairing a parked bicycle even when both have computers.
howTo: Define process monitoring and stop criteria

callout.text: Never scan, probe, patch, isolate, or reconfigure OT or ICS equipment as a learning exercise.

sections.title: Professional ethics and first-day questions
paragraphs: Professional ethics means acting within authority, protecting people and information, being honest about evidence and skill, avoiding conflicts, escalating material risk, respecting privacy, and refusing unsafe or unauthorized shortcuts. Curiosity does not override consent.

On a first day, ask before acting: What outcomes and safety obligations matter? Who owns systems and risk? Which policies, architectures, inventories, tools, data-handling rules, change paths, incident roles, vendor contacts, and escalation channels are authoritative? What should a newcomer not access or change yet?
keyPoints: Authority and competence are ethical boundaries
Honest uncertainty builds trust
Questions should discover local truth rather than confirm assumptions
sections.analogy: A new clinician first learns protocols, supervision, patient-safety rules, and records before treating anyone independently.
howTo: Read assigned policy and role material
Ask how decisions and escalation work

callout.text: Nothing here claims knowledge of ExxonMobil's internal technology, process, architecture, policy, or priorities.

sections.title: Five-week pre-start and 30/60/90-day plan
paragraphs: A five-week pre-start plan can build foundations without seeking internal access: week one reviews security and enterprise IT; week two networks and telemetry; week three response, intelligence, and forensics; week four vulnerabilities, applications, cloud, detections, and automation; week five OT safety, communication, and capstone rehearsal.

During days 1-30, listen, learn authority, complete required training, map stakeholders, and understand assigned services. Days 31-60 deepen supervised tool and workflow practice, shadow incidents and changes, and deliver a small read-only improvement. Days 61-90 validate a scoped contribution, gather feedback, document learning, and agree the next development plan.
keyPoints: Pre-start learning uses public material and labs
The first month prioritizes local context and relationships
Early contributions should be scoped, supervised, and measurable
sections.analogy: A new pilot studies fundamentals before arrival, then learns the airline, aircraft, crew, routes, and supervised procedures before independent duty.
howTo: Track questions rather than invent answers
Agree 30-, 60-, and 90-day goals with a manager

sections.title: Capstone: defend a fictional critical service
paragraphs: The capstone integrates the academy around a fictional water-distribution monitoring service with corporate users, an external maintenance provider, cloud analytics, security telemetry, and an isolated training representation of OT. It contains no real employer architecture, data, credentials, or equipment.

Produce an asset and data-flow model, risks and controls, connection review, telemetry plan, incident playbook, vulnerability priority, cloud and application review, detection concept, read-only automation outline, operating model, and 90-day briefing. State assumptions, owners, evidence, safety limits, and production approvals throughout.
keyPoints: Synthesis matters more than tool depth
Every recommendation states ownership and evidence
Safety and authorization boundaries are explicit
sections.analogy: A flight simulator combines navigation, communication, weather, systems, crew coordination, and emergency judgment without risking passengers.
howTo: Read the fictional brief and list assumptions
Build service, process, identity, and data views
Prioritize risks and design layered controls
Prepare response, validation, operation, and rollback
Present decisions, uncertainty, and next questions

callout.text: The capstone is complete when it shows sound judgment, safe boundaries, and clear communication, not when it names the most tools.

workflow: Prepare with public foundations and safe synthetic labs
Discover local mission, safety, authority, architecture, owners, and boundaries
Learn through observation and supervised practice
Deliver a small reversible evidence-based contribution
Gather feedback, document learning, and grow responsibility deliberately

quiz.question: What most distinguishes many OT security decisions from ordinary IT decisions?
options: Cyber actions may directly affect physical safety and process availability
quiz.explanation: Physical processes and safety consequences require engineering and operational context.

quiz.question: What is the best first-day approach?
options: Assume public diagrams match the employer
Learn mission, authority, owners, boundaries, and escalation before acting
Change a control to demonstrate initiative
quiz.explanation: Local context and permission are prerequisites for safe, useful work.

quiz.question: What is a suitable early-career contribution in days 31-60?
options: A claim to know every process
A scoped read-only improvement reviewed by an owner
quiz.explanation: A small reversible contribution builds evidence and trust while preserving supervision.

quiz.question: What should the capstone explicitly include?
options: Assumptions, owners, evidence, safety boundaries, approvals, and rollback
quiz.explanation: Professional defensive design is transparent about uncertainty, responsibility, and safe operation.

practice.title: Critical-service defensive capstone
practice.brief: A fictional municipal water-monitoring organization uses office IT, a cloud dashboard, a supplier portal, and an isolated training model of operational sensors. No action can reach a physical process.
tasks: Model assets, owners, IT and OT boundaries, identities, data, and supplier flows
Prioritize risks and propose layered safety-aware controls
Design telemetry, one detection, a hunt, and an incident playbook
Prioritize vulnerabilities and review application, cloud, and vendor responsibilities
Present a five-week preparation plan and 30/60/90-day briefing
answerGuide: The model distinguishes business IT, cloud, supplier, and simulated OT while naming unknowns and accountable roles
Controls address identity, segmentation, integrity, availability, monitoring, recovery, safety, and change
Evidence requirements, data health, test cases, severity, containment authority, recovery, and lessons learned are connected
Priorities use exposure, exploitation, consequence, controls, shared responsibility, validation, exceptions, and verification
The briefing is ethical, concise, role-aware, assumption-free about employers, and requests feedback
practice.safety: Use only the fictional capstone. Do not access, scan, test, or make assumptions about real critical infrastructure or employer systems.
